Existing optimizers often judge edits by aggregate validation performance, limiting the supervision they retain about which errors an edit corrects or introduces. Testing each candidate also requires rescoring validation answers, which limits how many edits can be explored within a fixed budget. We propose RubricWorld, a framework that learns from previous edit evaluations to guide further search. Its world model predicts an edit's correction and degradation rates at score boundaries, conditioned on the current rubric state. The training signal comes from paired grading results: scores for the same answers before and after an edit. Predictions select one candidate for direct evaluation, and held-out confidence bounds determine whether it corrects enough target errors while keeping new errors within prespecified limits. Measured effects update the model even when the edit is rejected. Across EIR (National), ASAP2.0, and ASAP-SAS with three frozen LLM graders, RubricWorld achieves the highest score in 20 of 27 metric comparisons. On ASAP2.0, it raises gpt-5-mini accuracy from 18.20% with the original rubric to 46.70%, exceeding the strongest baseline, APO, by 22.60 percentage points. code will be released upon acceptance.

papers.title: Same Trajectory, Different Knowledge: Information-State-Aware On-Policy Distillation for Search Agents
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation trains search agents with teacher feedback on student-generated trajectories. Recent methods augment the teacher's context with supporting evidence, reference answers, or hindsight information. However, this privileged information may allow the teacher to rely on facts that the student cannot reliably recover from its current state. The resulting information-state mismatch can lead the teacher to undervalue retrieval that helps the student establish those facts. To address this mismatch, we introduce Information-State-Aware Distillation (ISA-Distill), which adapts teacher feedback to the student's factual recoverability. ISA-Distill estimates how reliably the student can recover action-relevant knowledge and derives teacher feedback for the same sampled action from two complementary views. The fact-use view supplies the teacher with the relevant fact, producing feedback that guides the student in using knowledge. The evidence-seeking view instead presents the information need, producing feedback that guides the student in acquiring supporting evidence. The two signals are weighted toward fact use when recoverability is high and toward evidence seeking when it is low, and the resulting feedback guides policy optimization. Experiments across diverse QA benchmarks and model scales demonstrate improved answer accuracy and retrieval efficiency. Our code and model checkpoints will be open-sourced.

papers.title: The Agentic Observer Hackathon: Autonomous Decision-making in Simulated Astronomical Surveys
papers.abstract: Astronomical surveys must allocate observing time while responding to changing conditions and competing scientific priorities. We present the Agentic Observer Hackathon (AOH), a community challenge for studying autonomous survey operations. Within a synthetic multi-object survey with prescribed exposure responses and assignment constraints, decision systems select pointings, assign targets and choose exposure configurations while responding to observing requests, instrumental faults and data loss. We evaluate systems submitted by 102 teams on campaigns reserved for evaluation and analyse target completion in a reference campaign. The leading systems combine numerical exposure planning with language models for interpreting operational information and supporting longer-term decisions. Exploratory tests show improved fault reporting with model access in several systems, while revised scientific priorities produce substantial changes in ranking. The reference campaign traces target completion and diagnoses errors in the baseline's inference of prescribed quality bands. The released simulator and reference strategies provide common survey conditions for comparing exposure allocation, target selection and recovery from interruptions.

papers.title: Accelerating QUIC Encryption in WebAssembly Using WASM-SIMD
papers.abstract: WebAssembly (Wasm) runs untrusted code in a portable, lightweight sandbox and is increasingly used to host services on shared servers and edge platforms. Running the QUIC transport protocol inside Wasm would let each application choose and update its own transport without changing the host. QUIC, however, encrypts every packet, and Wasm offers neither dedicated AES instructions nor carry-less multiplication; a Wasm QUIC stack has been reported to reach only 17.6% of native goodput, with cryptography as its largest cost. Whether the 128-bit SIMD extension of Wasm (WASM-SIMD) can recover this cost, and what limits a pure-Wasm stack once it does, has remained unclear. Here we show that explicit WASM-SIMD kernels recover much of the cryptographic cost, after which non-cryptographic costs become the limit. On two hosts connected by 10-Gigabit Ethernet, kernels that process eight AES blocks or four ChaCha20 blocks per pass raise receiver goodput over a non-SIMD baseline by 61.34% for AES-128-GCM and 31.55% for ChaCha20-Poly1305, whereas compiler auto-vectorization gains only 1.28% for AES-128-GCM. ChaCha20-Poly1305 still delivers 1.99 times the goodput of AES-128-GCM, confirming end to end the preference that stand-alone cipher benchmarks suggest. Receiver-side profiling combined with Amdahl's law predicts that even native-speed cryptography would leave Wasm at roughly one third of the goodput of the fastest native stack. Cryptographic acceleration is therefore necessary but not sufficient: memory allocation, runtime overhead and per-datagram UDP I/O now bound pure-Wasm transports. We anticipate that this per-category cost breakdown will guide further optimization of Wasm network stacks and the design of system interfaces for batched I/O.

papers.title: Synthetic Realities: Evaluating Human Ability to Distinguish AIGenerated Videos from Real Footage
papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative AI have enabled multiple pathways for high-fidelity video synthesis: text-to-video, image-to-video animation, and video outpainting. Empirical side-by-side evaluations of how untrained viewers perceive and distinguish these outputs from real footage remain scarce. In this study, we systematically compare human detection accuracy across these three AI generation techniques within three thematic contexts: historical footage, film and media content, and natural environments. We constructed a balanced stimulus set comprising equal amounts of real and AI-generated videos (18 each). The AI clips were evenly distributed across the three generation methods using Google's Veo 3, Lightricks LTX Video, and Wan VACE. All videos were produced and standardized within the ComfyUI framework to ensure consistent quality and duration. 87 participants judged every clip in a binary forced-choice task ("real" vs. "AI-generated"). Participants correctly identified videos 60% of the time on average. Image-to-video clips were recognized most accurately (79%), followed by real footage (64%), outpainting (49%), and text-to-video (43%). Accuracy also varied by theme: film and historical scenes yielded higher detection rates than environmental clips, which were frequently mistaken for AI. Logistic regression confirmed significant effects of both technique and theme as well as their interaction (p < 0.001), indicating that detection success depends jointly on how the content was generated and what it depicts. Findings reveal a consistent bias toward assuming synthetic origins and highlight that perceptual realism in AI video is shaped more by context than by model type, underscoring the importance of media-literacy approaches and context-aware evaluation tools for navigating increasingly synthetic visual media.

papers.title: Weak-Signal Amplification through Stochastic Resetting
papers.abstract: Stochastic resetting (SR) offers a distinct route to amplifying weak periodic signals in nonlinear systems. Here, we demonstrate SR-induced resonance (SRIR) in a system with double-well potential driven by a weak periodic force, where the amplitude of the mean periodic response exhibits a pronounced maximum at an optimal SR rate. The underlying mechanism exploits dynamical instability: SR repeatedly brings the system close to an unstable state, where the phase of the periodic force at each reset biases the subsequent motion toward one of the stable states. The local instability then amplifies this weak bias into a large-scale response. The SRIR arises from a competition between rare resets that limit phase-dependent state selection and frequent resets that prevent the system from fully relaxing to the selected state. We develop a general renewal formulation for the periodic response and a coarse-grained approximation that predicts the optimal resetting rate, revealing the low-frequency scaling $r_{\rm opt}(ω)\proptoω^{2/3}$, in agreement with numerical simulations. SRIR is fundamentally distinct from conventional noise-induced resonance (NIR), which relies on noise-activated interwell transitions whose rates are periodically modulated by the external driving force. In the weak-forcing and slow-driving regime, SRIR can achieve much stronger signal amplification than NIR. SRIR persists for a finite spread of resetting positions, and our framework extends beyond bistability. We further discuss how SRIR and NIR can be selectively controlled. Our work proposes a novel approach to the classical paradigm of stochastic resonance.

papers.title: Cross-Dataset Generalization of Glaucoma Detection CNNs: Effects of Operating Threshold, Multi-Source Training, and Color Normalization
papers.abstract: Deep learning models for glaucoma detection are usually tested on images from the same dataset used for training. That says little about how they will work at a new hospital or with a new camera. We fine-tuned five ImageNet-pretrained CNNs (ResNet50, DenseNet121, MobileNetV2, EfficientNet-B0, InceptionV3) with identical settings on one of three public fundus datasets (ACRIMA, ORIGA, RIM-ONE DL). Each was tested on a held-out part of its own dataset and on the other two datasets in full. We used three random seeds and report mean and SD over seeds. Mean in-domain AUC was 0.913 and cross-source AUC was 0.702, a drop of 0.211 (SD 0.030; 95% CI 0.135 to 0.286). After correction for multiple comparisons we found no evidence that any architecture did better, though three seeds give low power. At thresholds set on the source validation data, specificity fell from 0.870 to 0.506 and sensitivity from 0.831 to 0.726. Resetting the threshold on 10% of the target images raised specificity to 0.670 but lowered sensitivity to 0.609, and balanced accuracy rose only from 0.616 to 0.639. Training on two sources together did not help (held-out AUC 0.695 versus 0.702). LAB reference normalization (cross-source AUC 0.755) and strong color augmentation (0.754) gave similar gains, cutting the drop to about 0.16. Ben Graham normalization (0.733) and CLAHE (0.712) helped less, and gray-world (0.696) did not help. The two best methods raised specificity but lowered sensitivity. On G1020, used only for testing, AUC stayed near 0.5 in every condition, and networks trained within G1020 were also close to chance. Strong in-domain results do not show that a glaucoma model will work on new data. Normalization and color augmentation reduce the drop but do not remove it. Studies should report external validation and check the operating threshold, not only AUC.

papers.title: Seeing Why: Exact Evidence Maps for Quantum and Optical Image Classifiers
papers.abstract: When an image classifier decides, we can usually only estimate why. For quantum and all-optical classifiers that act linearly on amplitude-encoded pictures up to the measurement, with no trained classical network before or after them, each class's Born probability above its no-information share, $P_g - b_g$, splits exactly into contributions of the encoded amplitudes, shown as Born evidence maps (BEM) over the picture. The split itself follows from known results on quadratic forms: with the transmitted light held fixed, it is what Integrated Gradients from a zero baseline and the Shapley value give. What we add is a way to measure it on the hardware that classifies, from class probabilities on a quantum chip or from camera frames on a lens bench, with no gradient circuit and no light sent backwards; a $g\times g$ map takes $1 + 2g^2$ runs. Deleting the 5% of pixels with the highest evidence drops accuracy from 73% to 9%, as occlusion does with 1,024 extra runs per picture, whereas gradient saliency removes much less. The classifiers share one architecture, a Fourier-plane mask followed by a brickwall circuit on qubits or by phase plates on a lens bench, read by a fixed Born headroom readout with no trained parameter; centring each picture on its own mean lets dark features count as much as bright ones. In simulation, four phase plates at a single wavelength reach 72.3% on Caltech-10 colour photographs. On IBM's ibm_kingston, with the mask applied before approximate loading, 300 test pictures were classified at 37.7% against 10% by chance (56.3% in exact simulation), and $2\times2$ maps of ten correctly classified pictures, one per class chosen by a stated rule, measured on the chip, agreed with the exact ones ($r = 0.77$). The maps also revealed a shortcut in the data; as the trim that removed it was chosen on test pictures, the Caltech-10 results are exploratory.

papers.title: Unfolding of symmetric monoidal $(\infty,n)$-categories
papers.abstract: We prove Lurie's proposed description of left rigid symmetric monoidal $(\infty,n)$-categories in terms of purely $\infty$-categorical data. More precisely, unfolding gives an equivalence between left rigid symmetric monoidal $(\infty,n)$-categories and complete categorical chain complexes of rigid symmetric monoidal $\infty$-categories. More generally, unfolding identifies skeletal sequences with categorical chain complexes without the completeness condition. We extend these equivalences to $(\infty,\infty)$-categories and, stably, obtain an equivalence between complete unbounded categorical chain complexes and left rigid categorical spectra. We also analyze their groupoid completion and express the homotopy groups of the associated spaces and spectra in terms of categorical cycles and boundaries. As examples, we construct the categorical chain complexes associated to geometric and algebraic bordism categories, including their equivariant variants, and to iterated span categories. Their localizations recover classical bordism and $L$-groups, while the span examples are related to algebraic $K$-theory.

papers.title: Rule-based hardware-configurable static analysis for quantum programs
papers.abstract: The rapid evolution of quantum hardware necessitates an adaptable static analysis framework for validating quantum programs. In this work, we introduce SHARP, a rule-based static analysis framework designed for OpenQASM that decouples hardware-specific constraints from the validation engine. By employing a rule-based approach, SHARP allows quantum computing services to validate programs against evolving instruction set architectures (ISAs) without having to modify the core analysis engine. SHARP achieves this by ingesting ISA descriptions as standalone data, making the validation engine resilient to hardware updates. Furthermore, the framework employs an analysis-driven validation mechanism that enables multi-stage validation, simplifying rule construction and enhancing extensibility. We demonstrate how SHARP supports hardware-specific validation tasks and discuss its impact on quantum software development, including language decoupling, program-level constraint validation, and feature access control. Our findings suggest that SHARP provides a path toward a scalable and maintainable programming interface for quantum computing.

papers.title: Safety4DM: A Vision-Language Framework for Risk-Aware Dynamic Maps in Vehicle-Road-Cloud Collaborative Driving
papers.abstract: Dynamic map (DM) is a core information infrastructure for vehicle-road-cloud (VRC) cooperative autonomous driving. It fuses perception data from multiple sources to overcome the inherent line-of-sight and field-of-view limits of single-vehicle perception. However, DM still falls short on driving safety in two ways. First, DM data specifications already define road conditions semantically, but no pipeline yet turns real-world road observations into fine-grained risk entities in the DM. Second, existing DM systems lack a natural language interface for driving risks. To close these gaps, we propose Safety4DM, a safety-oriented language system for VRC dynamic maps. We first build RoadRisk, a real-world road image dataset that covers four types of road conditions and four risk levels. On this dataset, we fine-tune a vision-language model (VLM) for road safety risk perception. The model outputs structured risk representations that the DM can ingest directly. We then introduce a Safety-aware Step-wise Prompting (SafeStep) mechanism as the natural language query interface of the DM. SafeStep answers queries accurately and also generates actionable driving advice. To build and evaluate this interface, we develop SafeVRC-Sim, a VRC cooperative simulation framework, and SafeDM-QA, a safety question-answering benchmark. Experiments show that even the compact Qwen3-VL-4B reaches 89.83% accuracy on risk perception after fine-tuning. SafeStep also plugs easily into multiple LLM families. With medium and large models (20B and above) from five families, it achieves over 93% natural language query accuracy in every case, which shows strong generalization.

papers.title: Boundedness from below in the real Weinberg three-Higgs-doublet model
papers.abstract: We study the boundedness-from-below (BFB) conditions of the quartic potential in the real Weinberg three-Higgs-doublet model (3HDM). Unlike an analysis restricted to neutral Higgs fields, a complete stability test must also allow for charge-breaking directions. We show that the problem can be reduced to a finite set of 28 stationary configurations, 14 neutral and 14 charged, each of which can be treated using a linear system of size at most four. The main simplification comes from the one-dimensional kernel of the Gram matrix for charged configurations, while the phase equations reduce to two possibilities: aligned phases or phases forming a closed triangle. We further show how to deal exactly with singular choices of the couplings by introducing an auxiliary deformation and taking an algebraic limit. For rational couplings, the normalized minimum is rational and an attaining field configuration can be constructed algebraically. We discuss analytical examples, exact checks, and comparisons with numerical minimization and StableWein. Our result applies to arbitrary real quartic couplings; it does not cover complex phase coefficients or settle the full-potential stability problem when the quartic is flat.

papers.title: Convergence properties of nonlinear RLC electrical networks
papers.abstract: Convergence properties of general electrical networks with grounded nonlinear capacitors at the nodes and nonlinear inductors and resistors at the edges are studied. It is shown how, under appropriate conditions, for every initial condition there exists a unique equilibrium to which the system converges asymptotically. Partial extensions to networks with terminals or current sources are also provided. For RC networks this is compared with the use of an alternative storage function based on the co-content functions of the resistors.

papers.title: Optimal Online Learning in Bilateral Trade Through Interest
papers.abstract: We consider online learning in bilateral trade on platforms such as Uber, Airbnb, and eBay. In each round, a platform posts a payment to a seller and a price to a buyer, both with private valuations, and observes only whether trade occurs. Its objective is to maximize cumulative gains-from-trade, the sum of the differences between buyers' and sellers' valuations across completed trades. We measure the platform's performance by its regret against the best fixed common price. Financial self-sufficiency motivates global budget balance (Bernasconi et al., 2024), which allows profits from some trades to subsidize others, provided that the final balance is nonnegative. Such financial planning should also account for the time value of money: profits earned earlier can accumulate interest, providing additional funds for future subsidies. Motivated by this observation, we introduce global budget balance with interest, under which a platform starting with no funds can use both trading profits and accrued interest to finance subsidies. For a horizon of $T$ rounds and a fixed exponent $θ\ge0$, we consider the per-round interest rate $r_T = T^{-θ}$. We study two classic valuation models, adversarial and correlated i.i.d., and obtain tight bounds on regret against the best fixed common price in both. As the interest rate grows, optimal regret in each model drops from $\tildeΘ(T^{3/4})$ to $\tildeΘ(T^{5/7})$. The intermediate rates differ: $\tildeΘ(T^{3θ/4})$ for adversarial valuations when $20/21 < θ< 1$, and $\tildeΘ(T^{(2θ+3)/7})$ for correlated i.i.d. valuations when $1 < θ< 9/8$. Finally, as an extension, we study $α$-regret, with approximation factor $α\ge1$, for adversarial valuations against the best feasible distribution over price pairs, and show that the optimal competitive ratio rises from 2 to 3 as interest strengthens.

papers.title: A Reider-type theorem for syzygies of cyclic covers of anticanonical rational surfaces
papers.abstract: Let $π\colon X\to S$ be a smooth ramified cyclic cover of an anticanonical rational surface, with $κ(X)\geq0$, and let $A$ be a divisor on $S$. We prove a Reider-type theorem for syzygies: for every integer $p\ge 0$, the adjoint divisor $K_X+π^*A$ satisfies Property $\mathrm{N}_p$ provided that $A\cdot C\geq p+3$ for every curve $C\subseteq S$ with $C^2\le 1$. One ingredient is a syzygy criterion for finite covers that reduces the weight-two Koszul vanishing on $X$ to weight-one vanishing for the nontrivial character modules on $S$. The most delicate case, in which $\dim|-K_S|=0$ and $K_S^2<0$, is handled by a separate geometric argument.

papers.title: TrackMem: Tracking Evolving Beliefs in Long-Horizon Financial Dialogue
papers.abstract: Memory systems for LLM agents are evaluated mostly on social dialogue, where facts accumulate and rarely change, so remembering reduces largely to finding the turn in which something was said. Financial dialogue breaks this assumption: figures are revised, stances shift without being restated, rules stated once govern later questions, and a single company is discussed under several analytical lenses. Memory systems that retrieve the passages most similar to a question, or the most recent ones, therefore return superseded values, miss rules that share no wording with the question, and cannot recover a stance spread across sessions. We present TrackMem, a per-speaker graph memory that tracks the history of figures, separates perspectives by entity and lens, and preserves each speaker's actions in chronological order. To evaluate it, we introduce FinLoCoMo, a benchmark of 15 long-horizon investment conversations with 765 questions in two splits: one following the LoCoMo categories and one targeting four failure modes. With two readers, TrackMem outperforms existing memory systems on both splits. On the failure-mode split it reaches 73.9% macro accuracy against 69.4% for the strongest baseline, with the largest gains on questions about revised figures (86.5% against 73.4%).

papers.title: To Align Long, Plan Short: Simulating Diverse Profile-Aligned Students by Realizing Short-Term Plans in Long-Horizon Learning Environments
papers.abstract: Simulated students offer a scalable way to test learning platforms and AI tutors before deployment with real students and to augment scarce data for studying learning at scale. Existing LLM-based simulators primarily target short, language-centered interactions. In open-ended learning environments, however, student behavior emerges from patterns across long-horizon interaction trajectories, where turn-level prompting can drift from an assigned behavior profile. We introduce ALPS (Align Long-term by Planning Short-term), a hierarchical simulated student conditioned on observable, environment-specific behavior profiles. Rather than selecting every action independently, ALPS alternates between planning profile-aligned task segments and generating the corresponding actions. We evaluate ALPS in both data-sufficient and data-scarce settings, where supervision comes either from real student trajectories or from a teacher LLM. Across both settings, we compare in-context learning (ICL), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reward-ranked fine-tuning (RAFT), and their sequential combination (SFT followed by RAFT). Experiments in an inquiry-based physics game and a pharmacy simulation evaluate behavioral density and coverage against held-out real data, and profile consistency using a human-aligned LLM judge. Across both settings, ALPS consistently outperforms turn-level generation, achieving comparable density and judge pass rates under scarce supervision, although coverage remains lower. These results show that hierarchical planning enables faithful, profile-aligned simulation over long interaction horizons, even with limited real student data.

papers.title: MIRA: Mutual Information guided calibration for Reliable Test-Time Adaptation
papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) updates a deployed model using only unlabeled target data, but standard entropy-based methods often rely on deterministic confidence and can reinforce overconfident errors under distribution shift. We propose MIRA, Mutual Information guided calibration for Reliable Test-Time Adaptation, a source-free online adaptation method that uses lightweight last-layer Gaussian perturbations to probe prediction reliability. For each target batch, MIRA reuses a single feature extraction pass and samples perturbed classifiers around the source classifier, forming an efficient local predictive distribution. Rather than fitting a Bayesian posterior, MIRA treats the perturbation scale as a local probing radius and selects a batch-specific scale using mutual information (MI) and prediction agreement. The resulting perturbation-sensitivity signal identifies predictions that are confident and locally stable under classifier perturbations, while suppressing brittle predictions with high stochastic disagreement. MIRA then performs adaptation with an MI-confidence weighted entropy loss, which down-weights perturbation-sensitive or low-confidence samples before they drive entropy minimization. This weighted loss reduces the influence of brittle predictions that can otherwise cause harmful adaptation under distribution shift. The method requires no source data, retraining, model ensembles, or offline posterior fitting, and can be applied as a plug-and-play modification to entropy-minimization TTA. Experiments on distribution-shift benchmarks show improvements in accuracy, calibration, and negative log-likelihood, suggesting that mutual-information-guided perturbation probing and weighted adaptation yield more robust online TTA than deterministic confidence.

papers.title: Polynomial convexity and non-polynomial convexity of totally real discs in $\mathbb{C}^2$
papers.abstract: We study the polynomial convexity of smooth totally real discs contained in the boundaries of strongly pseudoconvex domains in $\mathbb{C}^2$. Using Wermer's classical example, we construct a bounded domain with smooth strongly pseudoconvex boundary containing a non-polynomially convex totally real disc. We also construct a nonsingular Levi-flat hypersurface in a non-Runge domain containing such a disc. This provides a partial negative answer, to a conjecture proposed in an earlier work. Furthermore, we prove that the Wermer graph over the closed disc of radius $R$ is polynomially convex for every $R\in (0,1)$. Finally, we establish a sufficient condition for the polynomial convexity of totally real discs contained in the smoothly bounded strongly pseudoconvex domains in $\mathbb{C}^2$.

papers.title: A complete characterization of graphs with second largest eigenvalue at most $(\sqrt5-1)/2$
papers.abstract: In 1993, Cao and Hong posed the problem of characterizing graphs whose second largest adjacency eigenvalue is greater than $1/3$ and less than $(\sqrt5-1)/2$. Subsequent work extended the question to the non-strict bound. We give a complete structural characterization of connected graphs $G$ with $|V(G)|\ge2$ satisfying $λ_2(G)\le(\sqrt5-1)/2$. Their complements are described by disjoint unions of graphs from an explicit family with least adjacency eigenvalue at least $-(1+\sqrt5)/2$, possibly together with a cone or a thin or thick spider constructed from disjoint unions of members of the same family, subject to explicit numerical inequalities. This provides a positive characterization of the class, going beyond the classical result of Cvetković and Simić that the bound $λ_2\le(\sqrt5-1)/2$ admits only finitely many minimal forbidden induced subgraphs.

papers.title: The Carpenter property for subfactors of uniform infinite index
papers.abstract: We show that if $N\subset M$ is an inclusion of $\mathrm{II}_1$ factors of uniform infinite index, for instance an irreducible inclusion of infinite index, then every positive contraction $b\in N$ is of the form $E_N(p)$ for a projection $p\in M$. This gives the exact version of Popa's asymptotic result in the ultrapower, and it is a subfactor analogue of the Carpenter problem for masas. In particular, Popa's relative dimension set of such an inclusion is $[0,1]$, so the set of expectations of projections does not distinguish inclusions without corners of finite index. As applications, the Carpenter property holds for $N\subset N\rtimes G$ whenever an infinite group $G$ acts outerly on a $\mathrm{II}_1$ factor $N$, and for ICC groups $H\le G$ the inclusion $L(H)\subset L(G)$ has it exactly when $[G:H]=\infty$, confirming a recent conjecture. We also give examples showing that the Carpenter property does not imply uniform infinite index, and that infinite index does not imply the Carpenter property.

papers.title: Electroweak-Scale Cosmic Magnetism: Magnetogenesis, Baryogenesis, Phase Transitions and Gravitational Waves
papers.abstract: Magnetic fields, the baryon asymmetry of the Universe, and stochastic gravitational waves provide complementary probes of physics in the early Universe. Near the electroweak scale, these phenomena are not necessarily independent. The electroweak anomaly allows hypermagnetic helicity to exchange charge with chiral fermions, sphalerons can change baryon and lepton number, and first-order phase transitions in extensions of the Standard Model can drive plasma motion, magnetogenesis, and gravitational waves. In this review, we explain these connections and examine the literature needed to make quantitative predictions. We begin with the properties of primordial magnetic fields and the electroweak plasma, then discuss the mechanisms that produce magnetic fields, the conversion between helicity and baryon number, magnetic backreaction, and the evolution of the field to the present day. We also review the observational constraints and recent developments, including gauge-invariant descriptions of magnetic flux through the crossover and reconnection-controlled field evolution. Particular attention is given to the assumptions behind commonly used formulas and to the distinction between established results and model-dependent estimates. We argue that the most useful way forward is to predict the baryon abundance, present-day magnetic-field spectrum, and gravitational-wave signal from the same microscopic model, with consistent treatment of the intervening plasma dynamics.

papers.title: NAS-PO: Native Attention-Strategy Policy Optimization for Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an effective post-training paradigm for vision-language models (VLMs). Standard RLVR, however, assigns identical outcome-derived credit to all generated tokens regardless of their perceptual relevance. Recent perception-aware methods estimate visual reliance through image perturbation or masking. These indirect proxies require perturbation branches, while corruption sensitivity does not necessarily identify the visual evidence used for reasoning. We instead shape model perception through native attention, an intrinsic model signal. Rather than treating attention as a post-hoc explanation, we formulate it as a reward-anchored, token-aligned routing signal that encourages attention patterns supporting visually grounded reasoning. To this end, we propose NAS-PO, a Native Attention-Strategy Policy Optimization framework. NAS-PO analyzes native attention with a visual mass policy that quantifies visual allocation and a conditional visual policy that captures spatial routing over visual tokens, making the optimization well-posed. Based on this, Native Attention-Strategy Advantage Shaping (NAS-AS) draws on the visual-mass policy to redistribute signed policy-gradient credit for visually engaged rollouts. The Adaptive Attention-Coupled (AAC) loss then aligns the visual-mass policy on all response tokens and the conditional visual policy on visually active ones, consolidating the visual-routing patterns that drive successful trajectories. Experiments demonstrate that NAS-PO substantially surpasses leading RL-tuned VLMs across 7 out-of-domain reasoning and perception benchmarks, with its effectiveness consistently validated across 8B and 32B. Visual-Routing Sensitivity (VRS) analysis further indicates that the optimized attention prioritizes visually load-bearing regions.

papers.title: Retrieval-Enhanced Cultural Evaluation for Social Media Translation Training
papers.abstract: Social media translation requires preserving meaning while capturing the cultural nuances of user-generated content (UGC). However, gaps in the cultural knowledge of LLM-based evaluators can lead to inaccurate assessments and unreliable training rewards. To improve these signals, we use retrieval-enhanced cultural evaluation to train CUE-MT, a family of social media translation models. A calibrated, domain-specific Judger guides supervised data refinement and is augmented by an Agent for hard-example mining and reinforcement learning. The Agent retrieves relevant external evidence as needed and distills it into concise hints that the Judger uses to score translations and assign rewards. Across 9B, 27B, and 35B-A3B backbones, CUE-MT outperforms the evaluated open-source baselines of comparable size on CUE-MT-Bench and three public benchmarks. Human evaluation on CUE-MT-Bench shows cultural effectiveness gains of 7.44-15.12 percentage points over the strongest external baseline in each size group. Retrieval improves the Judger's four-way classification accuracy by 8.07 percentage points over a matched no-retrieval baseline that uses LLM-generated hints alone. Training ablations further support the combination of hard-example mining and Agent-enhanced rewards.

papers.title: Volume Doubling and Geometric Inequalities on Graphs with Bakry-Émery Curvature
papers.abstract: We consider irreducible reversible Markov chains whose nonzero off-diagonal transition probabilities are bounded below by $ε>0$ and whose reversible measure satisfies $m_-\le m(x)\leκm_-$. Under the Bakry--Émery curvature condition $\mathrm{CD}(K,\infty)$, with $K\in\mathbb{R}$, we establish Wang's log-Harnack inequality $$ P_t(\log f)(x)\le\log P_tf(y) +\frac{C\mathrm{dist}(x,y)^2}{\int_0^t e^{2Ks}\mathrm{d} s}, $$ for bounded positive $f$ bounded away from zero and all $x,y\in V$, where $C$ is a constant dependent only on $\varepsilon$. Building upon this inequality, we further prove volume doubling property: let $K_-:=\max\{-K,0\}$ $$ \mathrm{Vol}(B(o,2R))\le C_0\exp\!\bigl(C_1\sqrt{K_-}\,R\bigr) \mathrm{Vol}(B(o,R)),\qquad R>0, $$ where $C_0,C_1$ depend only on $ε,κ$. If $d$ is the maximum combinatorial degree of the support graph, we further prove under $\mathrm{CD}(0,\infty)$ the sharp volume growth bound $\mathrm{Vol}(B(o,R))\le m_-CR^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}$ for all $o$ and $R\geq 1$.

papers.title: MedPsy: State-of-the-Art Small Medical Language Models for Efficient Edge Deployment
papers.abstract: Medical language models promise expert clinical support, but the strongest open-source LLMs remain too large for private edge-device deployment, while compact medical models still trail substantially on knowledge-intensive and real-world healthcare tasks. Reasoning models that fit edge memory budgets can produce long reasoning traces, increasing sequential decoding, end-to-end latency, energy consumption, and KV-cache memory pressure. We present MedPsy, a family of text-only 1.7B and 4B medical language models designed for edge deployment, targeting this accuracy-generation-efficiency trade-off. Our recipe combines a synthetic medical data pipeline over biology, medicine, and health seeds with chain-of-thought targets from a 235B medical-focused LLM teacher; a four-stage post-training curriculum comprising two SFT stages followed by two RL stages with hard-sample mining; and an edge deployment evaluation spanning multiple GGUF quantization variants and real-device inference on laptop and smartphone hardware. On seven closed-ended medical benchmarks, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-1.5-4B by 19.34 points and matches MedGemma-27B while being 6.75x smaller; MedPsy-1.7B outperforms MedGemma-1.5-4B by 11.42 points despite being less than half its size. On HealthBench-Hard, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-27B by 15.33 points, while MedPsy-1.7B surpasses it by 11.66 points despite being ~16x smaller. Beyond accuracy, MedPsy reduces average response length by 1.7x (1.7B) and 3.2x (4B) versus its Qwen3 backbones, while Q4_K_M quantization preserves the aggregate score within 1 point of BF16 with ~69% lower disk footprint. In real-device inference, MedPsy-4B's shorter generations translate into 75% lower median end-to-end latency and estimated energy per answer than its Qwen3 backbone at matched quantization, while peak RAM remains below 5 GB across our tested laptop and smartphone configurations.

papers.title: A new class of optimal binary linear complementary pairs of codes
papers.abstract: The construction of optimal binary linear complementary pair (LCP) has recently attracted considerable attention in coding theory. Based on the Belov codes, this paper proposes a novel construction of optimal binary LCPs with $θ=4$, extending our previous work on $θ=3$. Our results not only yield abundant new optimal binary LCPs with flexible parameters, but also enable more optimal binary LCPs with smaller minimum distances.

papers.title: Randomized Adaptive Sequential Allocation and the Limits of Bounded Exposure to Inferior Treatments
papers.abstract: A clinical trial must learn which treatment is superior while sparing its participants from the inferior one. Kundu et al. 2025 recently showed that a purely deterministic rule, which always assigns the treatment with the larger current sample mean, achieves a strong form of this ethical goal. The smaller allocation count stays almost surely finite and has all moments bounded uniformly in the sample size. Deterministic allocation is, however, predictable, and predictability invites selection bias. We ask whether this bounded-exposure phenomenon survives once the deterministic rule is replaced by a smooth randomized one. We show that it does not. Under any fixed non-degenerate symmetric randomization, both treatments are sampled infinitely often, the adaptive sample means are strongly consistent, and the inferior treatment draws a strictly positive limiting allocation proportion. Consequently, the inferior allocation count grows linearly and its moments are unbounded. We then study annealed randomization, in which the randomization scale cools with the accumulated information, and obtain summability and divergence criteria that separate finite, sublinear, and linear exposure. A forced-exploration variant identifies the superior treatment with probability one while keeping the inferior exposure sublinear, and thereby frees the annealed guarantees from any correct-stabilization event. We also treat normalized multi-treatment rules, ties, indifference zones, unequal variances, general response distributions, and local alternatives. Finally, we develop the post-trial asymptotic inference that each exposure regime permits. The results delineate the trade-off between allocation concealment, persistent exploration, and ethical concentration on the superior treatment.

papers.title: The Coxeter-Todd abelian sixfold, Gamma00, and big Schottky
papers.abstract: We recall the construction of the Coxeter-Todd principally polarized abelian sixfold, and study its special properties. We show that the base locus of the Gamma00 linear system on the Coxeter-Todd sixfold consists of 253 points, disproving the stronger version by Donagi and Beauville--Debarre of the Gamma00 conjecture of van Geemen and van der Geer. This also leads us to construct explicit indecomposable 7-dimensional principally polarized abelian varieties that are not Jacobians, but lie in the so-called Big Schottky locus, thus disproving the corresponding conjecture from the Schottky-Jung approach to the Schottky problem. We furthermore show that while no even theta constant vanishes for the Coxeter-Todd sixfold, its associated Scorza quartic is identically zero. Finally, we show that there exist two different theta level (2,4) structures on the Coxeter-Todd sixfold, for which the sets of second order theta constants are projectively equal. This disproves the expected injectivity of the second order theta constant map for all genera starting with 6.

papers.title: One String to Rule Them All: Measuring Consent Under the IAB Global Privacy Platform
papers.abstract: Many privacy regulations, including the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA), require websites to honor users' opt-out choices. To facilitate this process, industry has introduced technical standards such as the IAB Global Privacy Platform (GPP), which aims to standardize collection and transmission of user consent information across multiple jurisdictions. However, it remains unclear whether these standards consistently and correctly transmit user opt-out choices, or whether opt-out choices are respected by advertisers. In this study, we conduct an in-depth analysis of consent propagation under the GPP framework. We collect data from four web crawls across four experimental settings to analyze how widely the standard is adopted, the extent to which opt-out signals propagate from publishers to third parties, and whether these signals reach and alter third-party advertiser behavior. Our analysis reveals several inconsistencies in the implementation and adoption of the standard that result in user consent signals being lost and user opt-out choices not being respected by the advertisers.

papers.title: Scaling Makes It Possible: How Large Models Master Impossible Languages
papers.abstract: While language models (LMs) excel in natural language tasks, their ability to learn impossible languages--those that violate the structural, cognitive, or logical constraints that make human languages learnable and functional--remains debatable. This controversy is further fueled by a divide between linguistic theorists and empirical researchers working with small-scale LMs. To address this controversy, we introduce semantic coherence. This concept measures how effectively semantic information is expressed in language structures and examines the learning capabilities of LMs across multiple scales. By fine-tuning billion-parameter LMs on impossible language samples, we demonstrate that larger LMs achieve similar performance on impossible and possible languages, whereas million-parameter LMs exhibit significant degradation when trained on impossible languages. This performance gap widens as semantic complexity increases. We further show that scaling up the LM size fundamentally shifts the learning focus from grammatical rules to semantic understanding, with billion-scale LMs exhibiting a threefold reduction in sensitivity to low-level linguistic perturbations while maintaining stable performance under high-level semantic perturbations.

papers.title: Improving Entrepreneurial Skills by Practicing with AI
papers.abstract: Durable skills like critical thinking, creativity, and collaboration are essential for innovation, yet teaching them remains difficult. In this work, we focus on the entrepreneurial domain, where these skills and others are required, and ask whether AI can be used as a tool for improving entrepreneurial proficiency. As a first step towards this challenge, we present an extension of Vantage, a platform developed at Google Research, adapted to serve as an interactive practice environment for entrepreneurship. Vantage pairs students with simulated AI peers engineered to navigate realistic business scenarios and challenge learners to exercise key skills. In a randomized controlled trial (RCT) embedded in summer entrepreneurship programs run by The Network for Teaching Entrepreneurship (NFTE), students using Vantage scored significantly higher on their Capstone Business Plans than control students with access to standard AI tools. These preliminary findings suggest that orchestrated AI peers can meaningfully support short-term performance on tasks requiring complex, durable skills.

papers.title: Switch-SWE: Do Coding Agents Hold Focus When Switching Between Unfinished Tasks?
papers.abstract: Software development sessions often involve several unfinished tasks rather than one issue carried through to completion. As coding agents take on repository-level development, they need to recover an earlier task's requirements and partial progress after intervening work. Existing repository-level benchmarks typically score one issue-to-patch episode and do not directly measure whether an agent can resume a task after advancing other unfinished work in the same repository. We introduce \textbf{\ourmethod}, a benchmark for focus-task resumption in sessions that interleave unfinished tasks drawn from the same source repository, with a persistent checkout for each task. Each focus task is evaluated in matched uninterrupted and switched sessions with identical focus requirements and executable verifiers. The switched session interleaves ordered stages from other unfinished tasks in the same repository, while only the final focus patch is scored. \ourmethod~contains 200 focus tasks from 19 Python repositories, reconstructed from issue, pull-request, and review histories and rendered as 400 matched session specifications. Across 7 coding agents, interleaved unfinished work produces an average focus-task resolution gap of 11.5 percentage points, ranging from 6.0 to 15.0 percentage points. Trajectory analysis identifies cross-task requirement confusion and loss of task state as recurrent resumption behaviors. We introduce a plug-in context-management module that selects task-relevant history and maintains concise task-state summaries. On OpenCode, the module improves focus-task completion under same-repository task switching by 5.5 to 15.5 percentage points across the evaluated models. Code is available at github.com/Miraclecsc/Switch-SWE.

papers.title: CULTURE-CMT: Benchmarking Contextualized Social Media Translation
papers.abstract: Social-media comments are interactions, yet they are often translated and evaluated as isolated text. This mismatch is especially problematic when meaning depends on surrounding discussion, community-specific slang, or culturally situated expressions. We introduce CULTURE-CMT, a Chinese-English benchmark for contextualized social-media comment translation that restores the post and conversational context naturally available to users. Its 572 manually verified examples are organized into Slang, Context, and Both, enabling diagnostic analysis of distinct and interacting sources of translation difficulty. To support scalable evaluation, we further develop a retrieval-augmented cultural-effectiveness Judger that combines a calibrated scoring model with dynamically retrieved cultural knowledge. CULTURE-CMT reveals several non-trivial patterns. Providing interaction context improves most model configurations, but does not eliminate culturally ineffective translations. Examples requiring both contextual grounding and culturally situated language remain substantially more difficult than either source of difficulty alone. Moreover, larger models are not consistently better, and thinking produces highly model-dependent gains, including occasional degradation. In contrast, a 27B model adapted on benchmark-disjoint social-media data achieves the lowest observed invalidity rate among the evaluated configurations under thinking inference with context. Together, these results suggest that realistic social-media translation is not simply a matter of scaling models or reasoning longer, but of learning to translate meaning as it is constructed within evolving online interactions.

papers.title: Multi-criteria Rating and Review based Recommendation Model
papers.abstract: These days, due to the advancement of information technology, recommendation system has become one of the key tools for e-commerce business. E-commerce platforms allow users to provide feedback in both written comments and numerical ratings. Recommendation systems are utilized to recommend users to new or unseen items based on these previously collected comments or ratings. In recent years, multi-aspect or multi-criteria based recommendation systems have been studied a lot by the recommendation research community. However, these research works are conducted either with reviews or ratings, not with both. In this project, we argue that integrating both textual reviews (with multiple aspects) and numerical multi-criteria ratings can further enhance the overall rating prediction accuracy. We propose a Multi-criteria Rating and Review based Recommendation model (MRRRec). We show that incorporating multi-criteria ratings into multi-aspect ratings from reviews has a great impact on performance. Our proposed model outperforms several state-of-the-art models such as ANR, DeepCoNN, and Deep Multi-criteria Recommendation System in terms of MSE, MAE, precision, recall, and F1. We show that our proposed model achieves an average of 19% and 23.0% lower MSE and MAE respectively and 7.0%, 1.0% and 3.8% higher precision, recall, and F1 score respectively. We further show that our model performs significantly better with Word2Vec word embedding than the GloVe word embedding method.

papers.title: Reverse Transportation and Harnack Inequalities for Underdamped Langevin in the Non-convex Setting
papers.abstract: We establish a dimension-free long-time reverse transportation, respectively Harnack inequality for the underdamped Langevin dynamics with non-convex potential. Specifically, we prove that for any two initial points $z,z'$ and $P_t$ the underdamped Langevin semigroup, it holds \begin{equation} \mathrm{KL}(δ_z P_t|δ_{z'}P_t) \leq C\mathrm{e}^{-χt}|z-z'|(\mathcal{R}\vee|z-z'|) \end{equation} for all $t>δ$ where $δ>0$ is arbitrarily small and $C=C(δ),\mathcal{R},χ>0$ are dimension free constants. In particular, our proof extends recent results which are restricted to either the convex underdamped or the non-convex but overdamped setting.

papers.title: ClickSight: An LLM Framework for Interpreting Student Clickstreams Through Learning Strategies
papers.abstract: Digital learning environments produce rich clickstream data that can reveal how students approach learning tasks, yet interpreting these fine-grained traces often requires substantial expert effort. We introduce ClickSight, a framework for interpreting student clickstreams through learning strategies defined in the literature. Given a student clickstream and a predefined set of learning strategies, ClickSight uses a staged LLM-based pipeline to identify strategy-relevant evidence, assess adherence to each strategy, and generate an evidence-grounded interpretation of the student's behavior. We evaluate ClickSight across two learning environments, 365 students, and 12 model backbones using an expert-grounded quality rubric and an LLM judge calibrated with human-expert ratings. Our results show that ClickSight can generate high-quality strategy-based interpretations across different models and environments, with reasoning models performing more consistently than instruction-tuned counterparts. We further find that providing external clickstream-extracted guidance can improve interpretation quality for strategies that require precise quantitative information from the trace. By connecting fine-grained clickstreams with theoretically defined learning strategies and preserving the evidence underlying each judgment, ClickSight provides a flexible approach for studying student behavior in digital learning environments.

papers.title: Topological Defect Statistics in a Weakly First-Order Phase Transition
papers.abstract: The celebrated Kibble-Zurek mechanism (KZM) characterizes the nonequilibrium dynamics of second-order phase transitions and predicts universal scaling of the average number of defects with the quench time. However, the KZM is not directly applicable to first-order phase transitions, where defect formation is instead governed by nucleation processes. Here, using a Ginzburg-Landau model, we investigate the defect-number statistics in a weakly first-order phase transition. We show that the resulting statistics contain signatures of both Kibble-Zurek dynamics and nucleation, revealing the interplay between these two defect-formation mechanisms. In particular, we find that the defect-number distribution evolves from approximately Gaussian to nearly Poissonian across the crossover from the KZM regime to nucleation-dominated defect formation. While the first two cumulants are well described by a simple additive estimate of the KZM and nucleation contributions, the third cumulant exhibits a plateau and an enhancement beyond this estimate, providing a sensitive probe of the interplay between the two defect-formation mechanisms.

papers.title: Naviq: An Open-Source System-on-Chip Simulator for Rapid Prototyping, Verification, and Design Space Exploration
papers.abstract: Modern FPGA SoCs are no longer just collections of accelerators on top of a programmable fabric. They combine programmable logic with hardened processors, NoCs, and components that dominate end-to-end performance. Evaluating individual pieces is insufficient; system performance depends on the interplay of SoC components. However, current FPGA SoC simulations provide limited support for this style of evaluation. Vendor simulations capture these interactions but are prohibitively slow for iterative design-space exploration. At the same time, generic software models overly abstract the hardware components that determine real behavior, resulting in less accurate simulations. Fast, easy-to-use simulators that accurately model real SoCs are critical for system debugging and design space exploration. We present Naviq, an open-source, cycle-level software simulator for FPGA SoCs, tuned to AMD Versal-class architectures. Naviq bridges accurate but slow vendor simulation and fast software modeling: it captures key behaviors of modern commercial FPGA SoCs while being fast enough for debugging and design-space exploration. Naviq models hardened SoC infrastructure in C++ and integrates accelerators through Verilator, allowing designers to evaluate custom hardware in a full-system environment. At the center of Naviq is an AXI4-compliant NoC model that captures transaction ordering, packetization, routing, backpressure, and memory interactions. Naviq provides CPU and memory integration, protocol checking, checkpointing, tracing, and performance-analysis tools for debugging and design-space exploration. Experimental results show Naviq closely reproduces the bandwidth and latency of Vivado's RTL NoC model while accelerating the evaluated simulations by 81x-182x. We present five case studies demonstrating Naviq's capabilities. Naviq enables practical full-system evaluation of modern FPGA SoC designs.

papers.title: Controlling the Sign and Magnitude of the Thermoreflectance Coefficient of Gold-MoS$_2$ Metamaterials
papers.abstract: Heating a material changes how much light it reflects. This effect, quantified by the thermoreflectance coefficient $C_\mathrm{TR}$, enables temperature sensing, while it is a nuisance for situations where constant reflection is crucial. Whereas temperature detection requires a large $C_\mathrm{TR}$, the latter situation demands it to be as close to zero as possible. Controlling the $C_\mathrm{TR}$ has so far relied on the selection of materials and wavelengths, rather than engineering the coefficient itself. This work demonstrates that the $C_\mathrm{TR}$ of a 50 nm thin gold film on SiO$_2$/Si can be controlled in sign and magnitude by an ultrathin ($<$8 nm) MoS$_2$ film underneath it. Time-resolved thermoreflectance measurements reveal suppression, sign inversion, and revival of the thermoreflectance signal, controlled by three knobs: ($i$) the buried MoS$_2$ thickness, ($ii$) probe wavelength, and ($iii$) ambient temperature. Transfer-matrix simulations using temperature-dependent dielectric functions of gold and MoS$_2$ reproduce all experimental observations, demonstrating an optothermal metamaterial platform with controllable properties. In particular, these (anti-)thermoreflective metamaterial mirrors bring $C_\mathrm{TR}$ under the same interference design rules previously applied to the optical response itself, opening ways to maximize or minimize the temperature dependence of the optical reflectance, tailored to the specific application.

papers.title: An entropic barrier to equilibration in the discrete nonlinear Schrödinger equation: Rigorous bounds for the microcanonical Brownian motion
papers.abstract: The relaxation of the discrete nonlinear Schrödinger equation is known to slow down dramatically when the energy density $\varepsilon$ exceeds a critical value $\varepsilon_c$, where the system enters a condensed phase. Replacing the Hamiltonian dynamics by Brownian motion on the microcanonical surface of $N$ sites at fixed mass and energy, we prove rigorous upper and lower bounds on the equilibration time $τ_{\mathrm{eq}}$, which is governed by the first non-zero eigenvalue $λ_1$ of the Laplacian on this surface. In the condensed phase the equilibration time is stretched exponential, not exponential, in the system size. The upper bounds on $λ_1$ come from trial functions: of one occupation for $\varepsilon<\varepsilon_c$, where the problem reduces to a Sturm-Liouville equation, and of two occupations for $\varepsilon>\varepsilon_c$, where they cross the bottleneck through which the condensate moves between sites. The lower bounds on $λ_1$ come from a Bochner-Reilly argument, with a vector field that compensates the concavity of the boundary. As a result, $τ_{\mathrm{eq}}=O(1)$ for $\varepsilon<\varepsilon_c$, while for $\varepsilon>\varepsilon_c$, asymptotically in $N$, $(\sqrt{2}-1)\sqrt{\varepsilon-\varepsilon_c}\leq\lnτ_{\mathrm{eq}}/\sqrt{N}\leq\sqrt{\varepsilon-\varepsilon_c}$. We conjecture that the left-hand bound is sharp and the right-hand one is not.

papers.title: Reconstruction as Spatial Evaluation: Diagnosing Cross-View Spatial Intelligence in Large Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: The spatial intelligence of large vision-language models (LVLMs) requires the ability to combine local visual observations into a geometrically consistent representation of the physical world. Many static benchmarks assess isolated spatial judgments, such as relative direction or distance, while interactive embodied evaluations combine perception with exploration, planning, control, and simulator-specific execution. To bridge this gap, we introduce RECONSPATIAL, a benchmark centered on multi-view 3D scene reconstruction across indoor, tabletop, and outdoor environments. Given real multi-view images and target-object queries, LVLMs are required to jointly predict oriented 3D bounding boxes in a shared, camera-anchored metric coordinate frame. Reconstructions are evaluated along two complementary axes: Structure for relative layout and Metric for physical scale and camera-anchored placement. Nine atomic spatial QA tasks, grouped into Geometric Perception and Spatial Relations, probe spatial capabilities involved in joint reconstruction. Offline navigation extends evaluation to path planning. Evaluation of 18 frontier LVLMs reveals a consistent gap between relative scene structure and metric reconstruction; even GPT-6-Astra scores 81.4% on Structure but only 58.7% on Metric. Tracing this gap, diagnostic analyses link atomic spatial capabilities to reconstruction quality and show that relational consistency alone does not ensure metric accuracy. Experiments with 3D map injection further separate scene construction from path planning, revealing how these geometric errors limit navigation success. Finally, spatial fine-tuning yields broad transfer across both spatial and general vision-language benchmarks.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware 3D Position Reconstruction in CZT Drift-Strip Detectors
papers.abstract: Accurate three-dimensional interaction-position reconstruction is important for CZT drift-strip detectors, but conventional methods can suffer from degraded performance in challenging detector regions, while learned models provide limited information about prediction reliability. We investigate two uncertainty-aware approaches: deep ensembles of point-estimation networks and simulation-based inference (SBI), which estimates a posterior distribution over interaction position. Both approaches are trained on physics-based simulations and evaluated on both synthetic and experimental data. On synthetic data, uncertainty from both methods correlates with positioning error, with SBI showing a substantially stronger relationship. On experimental measurements, the deep ensemble achieves improved $z$-position resolution, while SBI provides more informative uncertainty estimates that highlight regions of reduced positional information and discrepancies between simulation and the physical detector. These results demonstrate the complementary strengths of ensemble-based reconstruction and posterior inference for uncertainty-aware detector position reconstruction.

papers.title: LARK: Lean-Assisted Reasoning for LLM-Generated GPU Kernels
papers.abstract: Efficient GPU kernels are typically low-level and hardware-specific, and LLM agents can now generate them faster than experts can verify. Existing approaches rely on testing, which provides evidence but not a guarantee of correctness. We introduce LARK, an agentic framework that automatically and formally verifies GPU kernels against their PyTorch reference implementations. LARK proves equivalence in functional and memory behavior under exact arithmetic and establishes a new trust boundary: human effort is only needed to verify operator-level Lean semantics ahead of kernel generation time, instead of checking every single line of generated code. LARK formalizes the GPU machine model and the semantics of each operation in Lean 4 once per target language, and the Lean 4 semantics of any incoming kernel is derived from these pre-built definitions. LLM agents then automate the proof in two steps. First, an agent decomposes the whole kernel semantics into smaller segments and Lean 4 verifies this segmentation, which addresses the intractability of proving equivalence for large kernels directly. Second, agents write Lean proofs that each kernel segment matches its high-level PyTorch counterpart. Together, the two steps give whole-program equivalence. We demonstrate that LARK can be used 1) to ensure correctness in existing code-generation agents and 2) to automatically verify human-written kernel libraries. On the KernelCraft GPU tasks, combined with a simple ReAct agent, LARK enables GLM 5.3 to fully verify 10 of 12 Level-1 kernels and Opus 5.5 all 5 Level-2 kernels. Moreover, over 10 production kernels randomly sampled from popular open-source LLM serving frameworks, LARK verifies 9 and identifies a new data race bug in the tenth. We believe LARK represents a significant step toward verifiable code generation in the agentic era.

papers.title: Does Calibration Pick the Right Model? Likelihood Evidence from Income Risk
papers.abstract: Quantitative macroeconomics typically disciplines models by matching selected moments. We show how finite-state hidden Markov approximations make likelihood estimation and model selection feasible for nonlinear, non-Gaussian latent processes on short panels, without simulation. We illustrate the method with PSID earnings data. The calibrations that best match moments of earnings dynamics fit complete histories worse than a likelihood-estimated process with a Gaussian persistent component. In a standard saving model, calibrations of one process that fit the targets about equally well imply mean assets that differ by a factor of three. Close agreement with selected moments can leave economic predictions largely undetermined.

papers.title: Minimal Superior Penalties: Characterising and Calibrating Decision-Aware Proper Scoring Rules
papers.abstract: Training a classifier means letting a validation metric decide which model is kept and when training stops. A natural requirement on that metric is superiority: every correctly classified forecast should score better than every incorrectly classified one, however close the underlying probabilities are. Neither the Brier score nor the logarithmic score satisfies this on its own. We show that superiority is governed by the separation between two endpoints -- the supremum of the score on correct predictions and the infimum on incorrect predictions -- and derive both in closed form for each score. Their difference is the infimal penalty, the greatest lower bound on the penalty needed to restore superiority. Prior work restores superiority with a penalty calibrated from the first endpoint alone; for the Brier base, our infimal penalty is smaller than that published penalty by a factor ranging from 4.00 at three classes to 2.11 at twenty. We further embed the published and infimal penalties in a one-parameter family and show that, under a single-valued tie convention, every member of the family is strictly proper. In a pre-specified two-dataset case study, mean selected-model macro-F1 rises with the penalty in the reported ten-class regimes, though not distinguishably from noise once seed/selection-mode nesting is accounted for; a fifth regime at forty-seven classes does not reproduce even this descriptive pattern. The intended no-superiority baseline is algebraically a rescaling of the family under test, so the experiment cannot attribute the observed pattern specifically to superiority. When superiority itself is the objective, any penalty strictly above the infimal value suffices; choosing a larger penalty is a separate calibration trade-off rather than a requirement for the guarantee.

papers.title: Query-efficient scan-and-search watermark localization
papers.abstract: Recently, the detection of AI-generated content has been of particular importance in various fields of our society. For accountability purposes, many large language models (LLMs) have implicitly watermarked their outputs. Localizing such watermarks requires a piece of text to undergo an additional verification process. Existing localization methods typically rely on dense token-level scoring, making verification costly even when an LLM-generated watermark only sparsely appears. To tackle this problem, we design a new adaptive allocation strategy that first maintains broad document coverage and then progressively concentrates the detection budget on regions that exhibit stronger watermark evidence or are more likely to contain watermarked content. We then transform the statistical signals from the selected regions into e-values and employ the proposed token-weighted e-BH procedure to determine the localized watermark regions. The resulting framework is called BELL (Budgeted E-evidence Localization for LLM Watermarks). Theoretically, BELL can control the token-weighted false discovery rate (FDR) without independence assumptions across regions. Finally, extensive experimental results demonstrate that BELL consistently outperforms competing methods across multiple LLMs, datasets, and watermarking schemes.

papers.title: SensOFormer: Foundation Models for Particle Accelerators
papers.abstract: Large-scale scientific facilities, such as particle accelerators, are complex systems composed of thousands of interacting components that must operate collectively to support diagnostics and control, and ensure safe, reliable operation. These facilities rely on extensive sensor networks that generate large volumes of heterogeneous, incomplete, and noisy telemetry, often sampled at different rates across subsystems. In this paper, we adopt the foundation-model paradigm to learn general-purpose sensor representations from historical accelerator data through self-supervised pretraining. We introduce SensOFormer, a denoising masked transformer with a Perceiver-style encoder-decoder architecture designed to handle variable sensor sets, accommodate heterogeneous sampling rates, and learn robust representations from noisy measurements. The model is pretrained on multiple particle-accelerator datasets and transferred to downstream tasks, including missing-data imputation, anomaly detection, cavity identification, and fault identification. Through extensive evaluations and comparisons, we demonstrate that a single self-supervised model can learn reusable representations for diverse operational tasks in large-scale scientific facilities. Project page: https://mahindrautela.github.io/sensoformer.

papers.title: PRISM: RL-Based Rate Control for Low Latency and High Data Rate in Mobile Edge Networks
papers.abstract: Emerging delay-sensitive interactive services, such as extended reality and remote operation, demand advanced congestion control algorithms (CCAs) capable of maintaining high data rates while keeping latency low in mobile networks. Existing CCAs typically rely on congestion signals such as packet loss, delay, or explicit congestion notification (ECN) marks, which can be delayed, imprecise, or require extensive upgrades to the network infrastructure. To address these limitations, physical resource block (PRB) utilization has recently been proposed as a reliable early congestion signal in mobile networks [1]. This paper introduces PRISM, a reinforcement-learning-based CCA that uses peak PRB utilization to regulate the send rate under challenging mobility and fading conditions. NS3 simulation results show that, in a mobility scenario where two PRISM flows coexist with two TCP Cubic flows and one TCP BBR flow, PRISM maintains a per-packet mean one-way delay (OWD) of 6.3ms and a $p_{99}$ OWD of 44.6ms, with negligible (0.02%) packet loss, over a 20min high-contention interval. However, over the same interval, the coexisting TCP flows experience 60x higher mean OWDs of 371-390ms and $p_{99}$ OWDs of 563-578ms, with 0.1% packet loss. PRISM achieves a 31x improvement in goodput-over-latency performance, indicating a favorable tradeoff for delay-sensitive applications.

papers.title: How Green Is Your Manifesto? Scoring Environmental Positions in the 2024 EU Elections with an LLM Panel
papers.abstract: Locating political parties on environmental and climate policy is central to the study of party competition, yet the established instruments, expert surveys and the hand coding of manifestos, are costly, periodic, and slow to extend to new documents. We ask whether a panel of large language models can serve as a cheaper and reproducible alternative. Treating each manifesto as a set of sentences, three models from independent providers score every sentence on two dimensions, environmental protection and climate change, separating a party's position on an issue from the salience it gives it, and the judgments are averaged to the manifesto level. Agreement across the models is retained as a built-in reliability signal. We apply the panel to 41 manifestos from the 2024 European Parliament election, covering Austria, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, and the European party families, and validate it against the 2024 Chapel Hill Expert Survey for the 25 parties with a like-for-like expert benchmark, using the other manifestos as diagnostic cases. The panel recovers the expert ordering of parties with strong rank agreement on both dimensions, while reading them as systematically greener than experts do, a gap we interpret as the distance between manifesto promise and governing record. Inter-model disagreement modestly flags where the instrument errs, and position and salience prove related for environmental protection but independent for climate change. The result is a transparent, low-cost, and multilingual instrument that complements rather than replaces expert and hand-coded approaches; the prompt, code, and manifesto-level results are released openly.

papers.title: 4D Triangle Splatting Reconstruction of Dynamic Endoscopic Scenes from Monocular Videos
papers.abstract: Robust 4D reconstruction of deformable endoscopic scenes from monocular videos remains challenging due to non-rigid tissue deformation, illumination changes, occlusions, and unknown camera trajectories. Reliable dynamic reconstruction of endoscopies could significantly enhance visualization, diagnostic accuracy and intraoperative guidance of minimally invasive procedures. We propose SurgicalTS, a self-supervised triangle-splatting framework for dynamic endoscopic scene reconstruction from static monocular cameras. The scene is represented by a canonical set of triangles jointly optimized with a deformation network. We introduce a quaternion-based deformation model, an improved color parametrization, spatio-temporal priors, and a redefined initialization strategy that improves completeness under occlusions. Extensive evaluation on challenging in-vivo endoscopy videos from diverse procedures shows that SurgicalTS successfully models soft-tissue deformations and tool-tissue interactions over time, while consistently outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Our method also reduces training times while maintaining competitive geometric and photometric accuracy results, highlighting the effectiveness of quaternion-based deformation modelling with physical consistency for robust and efficient 4D reconstruction of endoscopic scenes.

papers.title: Spin-dependent topological structure of black-hole thermodynamics
papers.abstract: Thermodynamic topology classifies black-hole equilibrium states through topological defects of an off-shell thermodynamic field, while quantum-corrected Hawking radiation can retain information about the quantum numbers of the emitted particle. Whether these two structures are connected has remained largely unexplored. In this work we investigate this question for a massive-gravity AdS black hole by combining arbitrary-spin zitterbewegung tunneling with generalized-uncertainty-principle corrections. We derive the particle-spin-dependent Hawking temperature, construct the corresponding channel-dependent effective entropy through the first law, and formulate the associated off-shell free energy and thermodynamic vector field. As reference sectors, we also analyze the Bekenstein-Hawking and exponentially corrected entropies. We find a clear separation between local and global thermodynamic topology. For the $γ=-1$ branch, a single positively wound defect persists, yielding $W=+1$, whereas for $γ=+1$ the defects occur in oppositely wound pairs and the global charge remains $W=0$. The particle spin nevertheless shifts the defect positions and the critical configurations at which the $γ=+1$ pair merges and annihilates. The fold separating the two-defect and defect-free regions is controlled jointly by the particle spin, the GUP parameter, and the cosmological constant. Thus, the quantum properties of the emitted particle do not alter the global topological class, but they reorganize the local defect and bifurcation structure within it. Our results establish a direct connection between quantum-corrected Hawking radiation and the corresponding effective off-shell thermodynamic topology, showing that its local defect structure can retain information about the quantum channel through which the black hole radiates.

papers.title: Torsion, Frames and Quantum Bounces: Inflation and Ekpyrotic Contraction in Quantum Trajectory Cosmology with a Non-Minimally Coupled Scalar
papers.abstract: We study the de Broglie-Bohm quantum cosmology of a scalar field non-minimally coupled to a metric-compatible Riemann-Cartan geometry, comparing inflation with ekpyrotic contraction. The torsion trace is auxiliary and is eliminated algebraically before quantisation. The minisuperspace metric depends on the coupling $F(φ)$ and a constant $κ$ for an independent quadratic torsion term ($κ=0$ Einstein-Cartan, $κ\to\infty$ torsion-free). For every $F$, $κ$ and potential this metric is conformally flat, so torsion acts only through the Einstein-frame kinetic function $K(φ)$. Its curvature is therefore not a diagnostic of torsion, and the Laplace-Beltrami Wheeler-DeWitt equation, quantum potential and Bohmian trajectories are frame covariant. For a massless scalar the equation is solved exactly; in a two-packet state all 41 flux-weighted Bohmian trajectories bounce in the Einstein frame. In the Jordan frame the bounce at the symmetric event is independent of torsion and persists only for $ξ<ξ_c$ (closed form); torsion changes the late-time exponent from $1-\sqrt{6ξ/(1+6ξ)}$ to $1-\sqrt{6ξ}$. The bounce comes from interference in the state, not from torsion. For exponential potentials, exact Wheeler-DeWitt solutions show that in the sector containing the ekpyrotic attractor no Bohmian trajectory bounces, and single-momentum states bounce only where the potential is negligible and end in the crunch. For quadratic inflation the torsion-specific shift of $r$ is below one per cent. A single ekpyrotic field gives blue spectra, $n_s=3+2/(ε-1)$ and $r=16ε$, whatever the torsion, also for running $ε$. In an entropic two-field version the tilt shifts at order $\sqrtξ$ (non-minimal coupling) and $ξ^{3/2}$ (torsion). Tensor modes cross the massless Bohmian bounce almost unchanged and stay blue.

papers.title: Scalar Smoothness Is One Point on a Besov Spectrum
