The clean recipe passes quality and context-use gates across three Qwen2.5-1.5B seeds and on a 3.086B Qwen2.5 model. In an objective-matched comparison, cached and online targets are bitwise identical. Cached jobs are faster after materialization, but a 618.31 s cache-build cost prevents wall-time break-even through 16 measured reuses. Boundary-shift tests show tolerance to intermediate representation mismatch, and an interrupted block resumes to a bitwise-identical final state without rerunning unaffected blocks. In the tested pretrained-model conversion and distillation setting, cross-depth semantic dependence can move from online optimization into persistent data.

papers.title: Angle-dependent emission from evolving accretion layers
papers.abstract: Photon propagation through an evolving atmosphere can change the angular distribution of emerging radiation even when its integrated optical column remains constant. We quantify this effect in an irradiated, internally heated, expanding plane-parallel layer using grey, special-relativistic similarity solutions. The full angular radiation field determines both the source function and the acceleration of a pressureless flow in prompt radiative balance. We compare each evolving solution with two frozen transport calculations on the same density and velocity profiles, holding the source fixed in one and allowing it to relax in the other. Heating produces the familiar transition from limb darkening to limb brightening, while the temporal correction to the angular contrast changes sign with optical column. For an upper boundary moving at $0.04c$, an injection speed of $0.06c$, and heating four times the reference incident flux, the intensity ratio between direction cosines $0.1$ and $1$ exceeds the frozen, fixed-source result by $18.8$ per cent at column $τ_0=0.15$, but is smaller by $2.53$ per cent at $τ_0=0.55$. Source relaxation preserves this reversal. The corresponding direct photon flight times are one third and three per cent of the flow age in the oblique and normal directions, respectively. These solutions provide a controlled local benchmark for temporal angular transfer in evolving disc atmospheres and reprocessing layers; application to a specific accreting system requires thermal, spectral, and geometrical physics beyond the present model.

papers.title: Thermodynamic Underpinnings Affecting Compressive and Tensile Plasticity in Refractory Compositionally Complex Alloys
papers.abstract: Refractory compositionally complex alloys (R-CCAs) show great promise as next generation structural materials for extreme conditions, but alloys with excellent high temperature mechanical properties most often exhibit virtually zero room temperature tensile ductility, hindering potential commercial application. Several semi-empirical metrics have been employed for predicting plasticity in R-CCAs, including valence electron concentration, Pugh ratio, Rice criteria, and the D-parameter. While many currently available ductility metrics correlate very well when compressive plasticity is considered, only the density functional theory (DFT) based D-parameter shows a strong correlation in tension. A new ductility metric is developed using CALculation of PHAse Diagrams (CALPHAD) thermodynamics, Gamma, with includes the free energy difference between the body-centered cubic (BCC) and hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phases, the interfacial free energy of a (110) BCC surface, and an electronegativity-corrected lattice distortion. The Gamma parameter exhibits better correlation with tensile ductility than D-parameter and performs equally well in compression. While this improvement is modest, a thermodynamically grounded ductility metric is clearly required to capture intrinsic ductility behavior. Extrinsic contributions to brittle behavior in R-CCAs, namely interstitial oxygen content, are also briefly discussed. Combining the Gamma ductility parameter with CALPHAD-calculated oxygen solubility is proposed as a first order attempt to capture both intrinsic and extrinsic contributions to ductile behavior in R-CCAs.

papers.title: Depth Anyviewpoint? Evaluating Monocular Depth Over Viewpoint Sequences
papers.abstract: Monocular depth estimation aims to predict depth maps from single RGB images (forgoing the need for stereo camera pairs) and has seen impressive leaps in performance in recent work due to the introduction of affine-invariant losses and the use of foundation model features. These monocular depth models predict affine-invariant depth, which describes the relative positions of objects in the scene instead of absolute depth. While these models demonstrate strong performance on single image benchmarks and qualitatively consistent predictions in video, their effectiveness at preserving consistent spatial structure has been less thoroughly explored. Many potential real-world applications, such as handling video streams as input, rely on coherent three dimensional consistency in scenes. Further, anchoring relative depth predictions to a metric reference for a given scene is a key challenge for applying monocular depth models to real-world situations. We develop a novel evaluation protocol for monocular depth models using video sequences with moving camera positions to test the consistency of prediction across variation in viewpoint. We demonstrate this methodology over diverse, real-world video sequences where we are able to anchor depth model output to metric depth values using structure from motion. Our work demonstrates open challenges in the development of broadly applicable monocular depth foundation models, particularly with their ability to provide temporal consistency over long time frames. We also identify challenges in the straightforward adoption of structure-from-motion as a metric grounding tool for monocular depth estimation models.

papers.title: Learning from high-resolution 2D images to reconstruct 3D microstructures
papers.abstract: High-resolution three-dimensional (3D) microstructure characterization remains difficult to undertake at scale because volumetric imaging at the required spatial resolution is expensive, time-consuming or destructive. In many settings, however, fine-resolution two-dimensional (2D) imaging and lower-resolution volumetric measurements are both readily available. We introduce a Privileged Cross-modal Relational Distillation (PCRD) framework that leverages fine-resolution 2D observations during training to improve specimen-specific 3D reconstruction from lower-resolution volumetric imaging alone. We demonstrate PCRD on pultruded carbon fiber-reinforced polymer composites, using scanning electron microscopy as the privileged modality and micro-CT as the inference input. The framework transfers spatial organization by matching similarity distributions defined around corresponding spatial anchors in the teacher and student representations, avoiding direct alignment of heterogeneous feature vectors. In 2D cross-sectional reconstruction, PCRD improves mAP by 1.66 percentage points over direct micro-CT training. Independent 3D validation against high-resolution synchrotron X-ray CT data shows close agreement in fiber volume fraction, diameter and local spacing. The PCRD reconstruction matches 89.97% of the reference fiber centerline length, compared with 75.08% for the interpolated low-resolution volume.

papers.title: Fisher--Hartwig asymptotics and critical moments for the circular beta ensemble
papers.abstract: We determine the joint moments of real powers of the absolute value of characteristic polynomials in the circular beta ensemble, for every $β>0$. At fixed distinct prescribed points, the Fisher--Hartwig formula holds for every exponent greater than $-1$, with explicit constants and a relative error bounded by a negative power of the matrix size $N$. For approaching points in the same integrable range, the error is bounded by a negative power of $Nδ_N$, provided that $Nδ_N\to\infty$ and the sum of the absolute values of the negative exponents is less than two. Here $δ_N$ is the minimum distance between the prescribed points; this range includes every integrable pair of root exponents. For $q>0$ at the critical relation $pq^2=2β$, we prove the Keating--Wong asymptotic for the $p$th moment of the integral of the $q$th absolute power of the characteristic polynomial, for every real $p>1$. The leading asymptotic extends to every complex spatial weight in $L^p$. The proofs combine the recursion for orthogonal polynomials on the unit circle with conditional expectation identities for Gaussian multiplicative chaos and quantitative estimates for approaching singularities.

papers.title: Hardy transitions on product lattices
papers.abstract: Boundary conditions can change the dimensional scale of a sharp functional inequality. We determine this change for inverse-square Hardy inequalities on the product lattices $\mathbb N^k\times\mathbb Z^{N-k}$. Their sharp constants satisfy $C_{N,k}\sim N^2Ψ(k/N)$ uniformly for $1\le k\le N$, where $Ψ(α)\sim2α$ at zero. The law gives linear growth for a fixed number of positive coordinates, every intermediate power for suitable sublinear choices, and quadratic growth for a positive proportion. We develop a method that connects exact uncertainty inequalities with Hardy inequalities through logarithmic localization, and combines this transfer with a block decomposition to cover all proportions. The transfer holds on weighted graphs with an explicit geometric error and controls the variational problem over arbitrary functions. A mixture of two Mathieu ground energies determines $Ψ$. At the fully positive endpoint, the variational problem defining $κ=Ψ(1)$ has a unique nondegenerate minimum and a unique positive energy--moment minimizing profile. We also prove strict comparison with the continuum coefficient in every sector for $N\ge9$, the optimal uniform dimension.

papers.title: Built on Broken Assumptions (BOBA): Why Coding Agents Cannot Be Left Alone
papers.abstract: Coding agents are autonomous developers. Given a request, they change the code and report back when done. As such, they can handle not only independent requests but whole chains of them, each request built on the last. Agents are known to report wrong work as done, yet benchmarks still test them one request at a time, on human-written code, checked once. We build BOBA-Bench, 280 chains of 20 consecutive requests drawn from 140 real open-source projects, and evaluate ten coding agents on both. All ten do far worse on chains. On average, they complete 95% of requests taken one at a time, but when requests are chained together, they complete 51%. Worse code is not the cause. Once checked, agent code is nearly as good a base for later requests as human code. The cause is the mistakes agents miss. Coding agents declare a request done once their own tests pass, even when those tests miss a mistake. The next request then builds on broken code and fails about twice as often. The mistake is rarely found later. Nor can agents catch such mistakes by reviewing code. Asked whether an implementation is correct, they are right 53% of the time, barely better than a coin flip. Coding agents are therefore heavily dependent on access to verification. A single external ``that's wrong'' after a failed request and one repair round lift chain completion from 51% to 59%, and a repaired mistake no longer hurts the requests that follow. In simpler terms, coding agents are only as reliable as the checks they can reach: without verification, every request that follows is built on broken assumptions.

papers.title: Test-Time Scaling for Open-Ended Reasoning at Small Model Scale
papers.abstract: A vote over a model's samples can only help when the samples disagree. For open-ended generation the binding question is therefore not how to combine samples but whether a model produces samples worth combining, a question test-time scaling has answered for math but not for free-form text. We study it at small scale with semantic cluster voting, a judge-free aggregator that groups a small instruct model's samples by meaning and returns the largest cluster's representative, with no reward model or self-judging. On a 250-prompt benchmark with three tiers of answer checkability, the same pattern holds across three model families (Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.2-3B, Gemma-2-2B) and two generation seeds: voting raises accuracy on the math control, where samples vary but stay checkable (a gain of +10 to +29 points across the three models), yet adds at most +0.30 judge points on open-ended text. On a larger 200-problem MATH-500 run with the primary model, the math gain is +8.5 points (95% CI [+4.0, +13.0]). Almost every open-ended sample falls into one meaning cluster, so there is little to select over. The collapse is consistent with instruction-tuning rather than model size, and raising decoding temperature does not recover usable diversity, because it costs more quality than it adds (net -0.64 judge points, 95% CI [-0.93, -0.37]).

papers.title: From Fabrication Disorder to Quantum-Protocol Yield in Inverse-Designed Silicon Photonic Beam Splitters
papers.abstract: Telecom-band silicon spin-photon qubits offer a promising platform for scalable quantum networks and distributed information processing, but their fixed emission wavelengths require compact, low-loss beam splitters with precise splitting and fabrication robustness. Conventional designs can face trade-offs between footprint, optical performance, and wavelength-specific operation. Here, we employ adjoint-based inverse design to optimize photonic geometries beyond conventional layouts, developing 1*2 Y-splitters and 2*2 directional couplers for the silicon T (1326 nm) and Al1 (1482.44 nm) spin-photon qubits. The devices achieve footprints of 2.9 and 26 um^2, respectively, with excess losses of 0.14-0.44 dB and back-reflection below 5*10^-4. We assess fabrication tolerance using 100-realization Monte Carlo simulations incorporating etch bias, line-edge roughness, thickness, and refractive-index variations. Mirror symmetry reduces the splitting-ratio spread of the Y-splitter by a factor of seven to nine relative to the directional coupler. We translate these variations into dual-rail fidelity, ideal splitting-ratio-limited Hong-Ou-Mandel visibility, and random-number min-entropy. All realizations satisfy a protocol-performance threshold of 0.95. At 0.99, the tolerated splitting-ratio deviation shrinks from 0.035 for visibility to 0.0035 for min-entropy, and the simulated yields are 68% (T) and 91% (Al1) for coupler visibility and 90% (T) and 66% (Al1) for Y-splitter min-entropy. The tolerance of the target protocol, rather than the device alone, therefore sets the fabrication requirement for silicon spin-photon beam splitters.

papers.title: A Quasisymmetric Analogue of the Bruhat Order
papers.abstract: We define a quasisymmetric analogue of the Bruhat order on indexed binary forests using the multiplicity-free Monk rule for forest polynomials. For the finite window $\mathcal{P}_n$ of forests supported in $[1,n]$, we construct an explicit partition into saturated chains terminating at the top rank, proving that $\mathcal{P}_n$ is strongly Sperner. We also recover the known Catalan ballot formula for its rank numbers. For principal lower intervals, we prove that $[\varnothing,F]$ is a lattice if and only if it is Boolean, and characterize this property by the avoidance of a bent corner in $F$, a path of three internal vertices that changes direction. This gives a forest analogue of the pattern-avoidance characterization of Boolean principal Bruhat intervals. We also conjecture that every principal lower interval is shellable, providing computational evidence and proving the conjecture for a family of hook intervals.

papers.title: Forecasting Earth Surface Change in Embedding Space
papers.abstract: Repeated satellite imagery permits understanding of how our planet changes over time, letting us predict its future and plan mitigating actions. Most existing studies that rely on a time series of satellite observations forecast the spectral values at each pixel for a future target date. However, clouds, shadows, and sensor noise often corrupt these observations, so that spectral forecasters waste much of their capacity on low-level features or noise rather than real change. With the advent of Earth foundation models, we argue that forecasting in embedding space is a feasible and more effective alternative. To this end, we design a token space that handles irregular histories from different sensors and foundation models and supports forecasts at any query date. Tokens from this space are inputs to our proposed forecaster, E$^2$Forecast, which is a transformer with two branches: a Gaussian branch that directly predicts a mean point forecast and per-dimension standard deviations, and a rectified-flow branch that generates forecast ensembles. On Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 benchmarks, forecasting embeddings instead of spectral values halves the cosine distance (from 0.20 to 0.10) and greatly reduces overconfidence, lowering the z-score standard deviation from 2.63 to 1.22. By comparing new observations with its forecasts, E$^2$Forecast can also detect anomalous changes without labels or retraining, raising F$_1$ from 41.58 to 48.70 on a global benchmark. This consistent superiority is validated on nine remote sensing foundation models. Beyond change detection, we believe our approach advances the field by permitting effective reuse of diverse pretrained task heads. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ucam-eo/e2forecast.

papers.title: Empirical rather than simulated spectral band adjustment of MODIS to Sentinel-3 OLCI for European vegetation monitoring
papers.abstract: Spectral band adjustment derived from convolved spectra describes sensor differences under controlled conditions, but its applicability to operational products requires assessment. We compare this approach with adjustment estimated directly from MODIS and Sentinel-3 OLCI observations for European vegetation monitoring. Both streams undergo atmospheric correction and Ross-Thick/Li-Sparse Reciprocal BRDF normalization to nadir viewing and local solar noon. Using observations from 2019-2024, we derive annual OLCI/MODIS reflectance-ratio relationships with unadjusted MODIS NDVI. The operational correction uses quadratic red and linear near-infrared (NIR) functions. We compare these relationships with irradiance-weighted canopy simulations and assess the empirical correction at 460 locations. Simulated and empirical relationships differ, particularly for red reflectance at high NDVI. Background-dependent simulated ratios also demonstrate the limitations of a single NDVI-based function. The empirical correction reduces red and NIR root-mean-square error (RMSE) at 66.3% and 71.1% of locations, with median paired reductions of 5.98% and 13.67%. Median paired RMSE decreases by 0.86% for NDVI but increases by 0.95% for EVI2, 0.74% for NIRv and 7.07% for the Plant Phenology Index (PPI), calculated with stream-specific historical references. This study establishes an operational empirical adjustment and shows that the specified spectral simulation does not reproduce the relationship between the normalized products. It provides evidence for improved reflectance consistency while demonstrating that vegetation-index benefits require separate assessment.

papers.title: The nucleon is not a hard sphere: screening fifth forces with Skyrmions
papers.abstract: Laboratory searches for chameleon and symmetron fifth forces increasingly rely on individual nucleons as sources or probes, but model them as uniform spheres. Motivated by the Skyrme picture, we instead consider a nucleon profile with a constant-density core and an $r^{-6}$ pion tail, together with its exponential truncation at the physical pion mass. We derive analytic screening charges for the uniform sphere and the $r^{-6}$ profile, and extend the comparison to the exponential truncation at the physical pion mass using numerical solutions. Because the outer tail is too dilute to be screened at any coupling strength, the $r^{-6}$ tail produces a power-law enhancement over the sphere charge in strong screening, and the exponential tail has a weaker, logarithmic enhancement. Propagating this difference through the published analyses, nucleon-sourced exclusion regions extend systematically further into the strongly coupled regime. For example, symmetron constraints from neutron interferometry at $μ=1\,\mathrm{keV}$ reach maximal self-couplings about $1.4$ orders of magnitude higher than for a uniform-sphere neutron ($3.0$ orders of magnitude in the chiral limit),and at the dark-energy scale the hydrogen $1s$--$2s$ chameleon bound reaches couplings $1.8$ orders of magnitude weaker than for a uniform-sphere proton ($2.4$ in the chiral limit), overtaking the muonium bound.

papers.title: Clock Offsets and Ranges from Optical Pseudoranges
papers.abstract: This note describes the estimation of ranges and clock offsets from measured pseudoranges in the context of the Kepler Navigation System. The latter system continuously adapts the frequency of its clocks to ensure that they all show the same time independently of where they are. In Medium Earth Orbits, the joint problem of estimating ranges and clock offsets can then be factorized.

papers.title: Discrimination, Calibration, and Ranking: A Unified Matrix Framework
papers.abstract: Discrimination, calibration, and ranking are the three pillars of classifier evaluation, yet no single algebraic language spans all three. A recent indicator-matrix account unifies discrimination measures (precision, recall, F1, Matthews correlation) across binary, multiclass, multilabel and related settings, using Boolean cell operations on indicator label matrices, generalised to soft labels by t-norms. Calibration measures (Brier score, log-loss) and ranking measures (nDCG, AUC) fall outside it. We close the gap with two further classes of cell operators: deviation operators phi(y - yhat), which give a Calibration Framework, and rank- and slice-dependent operators (positional gains for DCG, column concordance cells for AUC), which give a Ranking Framework. Both inherit the micro/macro/exemplar aggregation architecture. For calibration, the three Brier aggregations collapse to one scalar; the Murphy decomposition holds in matrix form (unbinned, binned and isotonic); and, within the Brier-type class-indexed family, a measure is skew-invariant if and only if it depends only on the class-conditional errors alpha_j and beta_j, the calibration analogues of recall and specificity. For ranking, raw DCG collapses across aggregations while nDCG does not; per-class nDCG and per-class AUC are related by a row-column duality; micro-AUC differs from pooled ROC-AUC; raw positional scores are never strictly proper, and nDCG and AUC need not be proper. The skew-invariant per-class building blocks share one class-conditional expectation template. Experiments on two multilabel benchmarks illustrate the distinctions. Many of the results are machine-checked in Lean 4; the proofs, the experiments and the aggmetrics.scores package are public: https://github.com/rcprati/discrimination-calibration-ranking

papers.title: Do agents need to sleep?
papers.abstract: LLM-based agents, which increasingly operate persistently across sessions and accumulate memory through interaction, already exhibit the familiar symptoms of unchecked plasticity: semantic drift, degraded retrieval precision, propagation of stored errors, and saturation of memory capacity. Drawing on the selectionist "ringing, resonance and renormalization" (RRR) account of sleep, we propose that each of its three phases maps onto an operation feasible in digital memory architectures. Engineers building stateful agents, meanwhile, are independently rediscovering the problems sleep evolved to solve: what to forget, and when to do the forgetting. From this we derive the falsifiable prediction that selectionist consolidation will outperform instructionist alternatives as memory stores grow large. The core claim concerns the nature of continuous learning itself: plasticity has a price, and for any system that learns continuously under finite capacity while coupled to its environment, that price is sleep.

papers.title: A converse theorem for GL(2) over global fields without root numbers
papers.abstract: We prove a converse theorem for GL(2) over global fields in which the root numbers in the twisted functional equations need not be prescribed. Instead, we allow nonzero scalar factors that are invariant under unramified twists. We show that these scalars are independent of the twisting character and obtain a unique isobaric automorphic representation with the prescribed unramified local components.

papers.title: Beyond Ensemble Disagreement: Predictive STL Monitoring of RL Locomotion under Distribution Shift
papers.abstract: RL locomotion policies trained under nominal simulation conditions may encounter distribution shifts that compromise safety. Predictive monitors could anticipate violations, but their world-model forecasts may become unreliable under shift, and ensemble disagreement is not calibrated. We evaluate predictive Signal Temporal Logic (STL) monitoring for frozen Ant-v5 and HalfCheetah-v5 policies using closed-loop world-model rollouts and a three-model ensemble. Across external-force, observation-noise, and mass shifts, predicted robustness ranks HalfCheetah's future STL violations strongly, whereas disagreement does not reliably track observation prediction error or violations. Under severe noise, violations remain common ($64.2\pm24.4\%$ at $K{=}20$ across three PPO seeds), yet current-state robustness without prediction comes within $0.03$ AUROC of predictive robustness. Penalizing predicted robustness by disagreement does not consistently improve ranking. Ant provides complementary per-specification evidence, but its composite target has no positive violations and its any-violation target is single-class in most evaluated seed-condition slices. Overall, predictive robustness provides useful STL-specific ranking but little demonstrated additional ranking value over the current state; these findings caution against treating ensemble disagreement as a reliable indicator of safety uncertainty.

papers.title: What is the connection between quantum relationality and symmetry-based relationality?
papers.abstract: Although it has often been noted that both quantum mechanics and relativistic physics involve significant forms of relationality, the nature of the connection remains unclear. In addressing such a question it makes sense to start from the simplest possibility, so in this article I set out to consider the viability of the hypothesis that the two types of relationality are ultimately the same: that is, quantum states always characterize degrees of freedom which can be changed by a symmetry transformation, so they are relativized for exactly the same reason as partial observables in general relativity. I use the idea that we only measure partial observables to argue that this suggestion is compatible with all existing empirical evidence for quantum mechanics, and then I consider the consequences for ongoing debates about the nature of measurement in quantum mechanics.

papers.title: Statistical mechanics of spontaneous behavior
papers.abstract: Why do a few behaviors fill most of an animal's time? The usual answer is that these behaviors are started more often, because learning and reinforcement favor them. Here we show that how long a behavior lasts can, by itself, explain much of what is observed. We consider a system that runs until it meets a constraint, such as a wall, and then resets. The fraction of time it spends in each behavior then follows the Boltzmann law, and the partition function is the mean time between resets. The four laws of thermodynamics follow as theorems from four postulates, and critical points that act as bottlenecks become the most occupied states. In 47 multi-day recordings of fruit flies, the dominant behavior accounts for only $13\%$ of bout starts yet fills $49\%$ of the time, and its typical duration identifies the individual fly. These results lay the groundwork for a statistical mechanics of behavior.

papers.title: Solving the Mystery of the Electron Radiation Belt at Uranus: Leveraging Knowledge of Earth's Radiation Belts in a Re-Examination of Voyager 2 Observations
papers.abstract: Voyager 2 provided the only direct measurement of the radiation environment at Uranus and established the well-accepted characterization of a system with a weaker ion radiation belt and surprisingly intense electron radiation belt. Recent re-analysis of the flyby, however, suggests that these observations were not taken during normal solar wind conditions, and instead occurred while a large solar wind transient, a corotating interaction region, was passing over the system. With this context, this study compares the Voyager 2 observations to a similar event observed at Earth. This comparative approach, along with an expanded contextual interpretation of the Voyager 2 flyby, suggests that solar wind-magnetospheric interactions at Uranus may have driven enhanced lower band chorus wave emissions capable of accelerating electrons to relativistic energies. This motivates new, more expansive questions to be explored at Uranus and highlights the need for a Uranus orbiter mission.

papers.title: A Data-Driven, Gain-Scheduled Equivalent Circuit for the B-H Behavior of Power Ferrites
papers.abstract: An equivalent circuit for the dynamic B-H behavior of power ferrites is identified from measured transients. It consists of classical elements of hysteresis modeling: a nonlinear inductor for the reversible curve, six viscous play branches (inductors in series with diode-bridge sliders) that form a Prandtl-Ishlinskii model, two R-L branches for the magnetic after-effect, a mean-field feedback of H as in the Jiles-Atherton model, and a measurement path. All elements are positive apart from the feedback sources, and the circuit can run in SPICE. Discretized at the sampling step, the circuit is a difference equation with 32 parameters per material, fitted by backpropagation through time. On the 15 materials of the MagNet Challenge 2, the mean sequence relative error is 7.33 % against 7.77 % for the challenge-winning recurrent network with 336 parameters, and the circuit is more accurate on 12 of the 15 materials. The accuracy can be scaled up by gain scheduling, where a small network per material sets the element values at every step from the excitation, while the hysteresis memory stays in the circuit, such that the error drops to 5.25 % with 656 parameters per material. Thus, an interpretable model is demonstrated that achieves state-of-the-art accuracy.

papers.title: On the probability that the integer parts of polynomials are coprime
papers.abstract: We prove that for any $s\ge 2$ and polynomials $f_{1}(x),\dots,f_{s-1}(x)\in \mathbb{R}[x]$ satisfying a certain equidistribution condition, the natural density of the numbers $n\in \mathbb{N}$ such that $n,\lfloor f_{1}(n)\rfloor,\dots,\lfloor f_{s-1}(n)\rfloor$ are mutually coprime is $1/ζ(s)$. This generalises a recent result of Champagne, in which this was proven under the assumption that $f_{1}$ is linear.

papers.title: Radial Evolution of a CIR: Observations From a Nearly Radially Aligned Event Between Parker Solar Probe and STEREO-A
papers.abstract: The addition of Parker Solar Probe (PSP) to the Heliophysics System Observatory has allowed for the unprecedented ability to study Corotating Interaction Regions (CIRs) at multiple radial distances without significant temporal/longitudinal variations. On September 19, 2019, PSP observed a CIR at $\sim$0.5 au when it was nearly radially aligned with the Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory-Ahead (STEREO-A) spacecraft at $\sim$1 au, allowing for an unambiguous assessment of the radial evolution of a single CIR. Bulk plasma and magnetic field signatures of the CIR evolve in a fashion characteristic to previous observations; however, the suprathermal ions are enhanced over a larger longitudinal range at PSP than at STEREO-A, although at much lower intensities. The longitudinal spread appears to be largely a consequence of magnetic field line topology at CIRs between the compressed slow solar wind upstream and high-speed stream following the CIR, underscoring the importance of the large-scale topology of these structures.

papers.title: Nondestructive 3D Metrology of Through-Glass Via Geometry and Internal Wall Texture Using Holotomography
papers.abstract: Through-glass vias (TGVs) are increasingly important for semiconductor packaging, yet their internal geometry and wall texture remain difficult to characterize nondestructively. Here, we use holotomography (HT) to inspect the three-dimensional (3D) geometry and internal wall texture of intact, unfilled TGVs before metallization. HT reconstructs the refractive index (RI) distribution of the glass and via. Maps of RI and spatially filtered RI then localize the internal boundary. Geometric fitting quantifies via dimensions and taper, while spatial filtering separates slowly varying wall form from finer texture. The reconstructed surface supports volumetric visualization, dimensional measurements and spatial characterization of wall texture within one optical inspection workflow. These measurements reveal internal features inaccessible from surface views and provide quantitative descriptors to evaluate TGVs

papers.title: Modeling and Experimental Validation of Bubble-Induced Performance Losses in Microstructured Copper Electrodes for Alkaline Water Electrolysis
papers.abstract: Water electrolysis is a promising technology for sustainable hydrogen (H$_2$) production. However, gas bubble formation significantly degrades the electrochemical surface area ($A_{\rm EC}$) and the electrocatalytic activity of microstructured electrodes in water electrolyzer cells. Existing theoretical models fail to connect computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and electrochemistry to analyze how bubble dynamics affect the performance of gas-evolving microstructured electrodes. This work develops a multiphysics-based theoretical model that couples two-phase CFD with Butler-Volmer and Faradaic kinetics, incorporating exchange current density, cell current, gravitational acceleration, surface tension, and fluid properties such as density and viscosity. The model quantifies essential electrochemical parameters, such as the enhancement in $A_{\rm EC}$ and the overpotential ($η$), which deviate by less than 7\% and 15\%, respectively, from the experimental results. Evaluations of the fabricated microstructured electrodes using polarization curves, cyclic voltammetry, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, and linear polarization resistance techniques demonstrate reduced $η$ by 2.49--21.39\% and 9.55--24.32\% for oxygen (O$_2$) and H$_2$ evolution, respectively. Furthermore, the model reveals the interplay between enhanced geometric surface area and bubble-transport limitations, facilitating the optimization and analysis of structural parameters. These findings establish a physics-informed roadmap for designing optimal, robust, and industry-scalable microstructured electrodes for efficient H$_2$ generation via water electrolysis.

papers.title: Quantum Temporal Marginal Problem
papers.abstract: Experiments on a multi-time quantum process may reveal its responses only on selected, possibly overlapping, sets of times. We ask whether these partial descriptions admit a common underlying process, and formulate this process tensor marginal problem as a semidefinite feasibility test. Agreement on overlaps is necessary but insufficient: three locally consistent qubit marginals can have no common extension. Another family is incompatible as a time-ordered process even though a single quantum channel satisfies both its channel and temporal marginal constraints. This isolates temporal causality as the obstruction. We quantify incompatibility by the mixing needed to restore compatibility and derive finite tests using separate interventions at each time and final measurements. We further show that incompatibility is equivalent to an advantage over every compatible family in a multi-time process-discrimination task. Together, these results test whether process descriptions obtained in different experiments can arise from one causally ordered quantum process.

papers.title: Integrating Data Center Flexibility into Power System Operations: A Framework for Temporal Redispatch
papers.abstract: Rapid growth in data center electricity demand, driven by artificial intelligence (AI) training and inference, is expected to increase stress conditions for power grids. Operational flexibility from data centers offers a near-term lever to relieve such stresses. Existing models of data center flexibility tend to bundle economic incentives with physical constraints, obscuring the tradeoff between economic willingness to shift load and technical limitations to do so. This paper proposes a temporal-redispatch focused framework that decouples data center demand flexibility into two independently parameterized dimensions: (1) systematic flexibility, capturing the economic environment through penalties for temporal shifting of data centers' scheduled demand, and (2) operational flexibility, capturing the physical envelope through the demand shifting time window and the limit on shifted data center demand. The framework relies on a direct current optimal power flow (DC-OPF) linear program which enables annual parametric analysis at hourly resolution. The framework is studied using a synthetic grid mimicking the Texas transmission system populated with the 2026 Adjusted Forecast from ERCOT (Electric Reliability Council of Texas). Results show that operational flexibility imposes a physical lower bound on unsatisfied demand that no economic incentive can overcome; longer shifting windows and higher limits on shifted data center demand reduce operational cost with different impacts on grid utilization; and, temporal redispatch shaves system-wide net load peaks while partially compensating for localized transmission bottlenecks that emerge under modeled coal retirement scenarios.

papers.title: Generalized Quasi-Symmetric Nets: A Constructive Approach to the Equimodular Elliptic Type and to Flexible $m \times n$ Nets
papers.abstract: Quadrilateral meshes that flex with rigid planar faces are of interest to transformable architecture, rigid-foldable origami, and mechanical metamaterials. Their building blocks are flexible $3 \times 3$ nets, that is, Kokotsakis polyhedra with a quadrangular base, classified by Izmestiev. We study one of his types, the equimodular elliptic type, defined by three conditions on the flat angles, the third of them through Jacobi elliptic functions. We turn these conditions into equivalent algebraic ones, free of elliptic functions, which lead to the generalized quasi-symmetric nets (GQS-nets), polyhedra of this type that include the known elliptic quasi-symmetric nets. For every polyhedron of this type, we give a flexible polyhedron with the same flat angles and its flexion in closed form. From the simplest GQS-nets, we assemble arbitrarily large flexible $m \times n$ nets. Examples include nets that, at one position, form letters; further nets in the supplementary materials form digits or, seen along their rows, approximately follow the side silhouettes of a bunny and a fish. Unlike numerically computed mechanisms, these nets are exactly flexible. As an application, we design three such nets as transportable arch halls of 80 mm sandwich panels, which fold to fit through the door of a standard container or into the well of a low-bed semi-trailer, and we check them numerically under snow load and build a 1:20 model of one. Supplementary Mathematica notebooks verify the symbolic computations, a Python tool constructs the nets and checks them numerically, including for self-intersections, and further scripts recheck the halls.

papers.title: Who Should Score the Cache? Mid-Depth Layers Are the Best Judges of KV-Cache Eviction
papers.abstract: Key-value (KV) cache eviction methods rank tokens by attention scores, and each layer scores its own cache. To our knowledge, no eviction method asks which layer should score. We find, across twenty-one models, that the depth of the scoring layer governs eviction quality. On the eighteen models with per-layer caches, spanning 0.5B to 109B, long-context retrieval accuracy collapses at shallow layers, peaks between 0.4 and 0.75 of depth, and degrades at the last layer. The curve arises because a layer judges tokens well only once it has used the question to find the answer, which takes several layers. Modeling eviction as a top-$k$ cut, we compute answer survival probability from prefill attention and reproduce the measured curves. This approach selects the scoring layer using calibration prompts with known answers, and the selected layer is the best layer measured on most models and never significantly below it. It improves on the own-layer default on sixteen of the eighteen models, with significant gains on seven, all at 14B or below, while on larger models the default is already close to the best mid-depth layer. Scoring every cache from the selected layer while keeping one set of tokens for all heads also beats per-head SnapKV by 18 to 43 points on five models up to 14B under tight budgets. This gain carries over to financial filings at 32K context, all at the same memory budget, with no extra forward pass. The same curve explains a penalty in shared-cache models, where several layers read one cache and the layer that writes it scores by default. On Gemma-4-E2B the writer is shallow and loses 28 points to a mid-depth reader at a 10% budget. We also find that in open-book question answering (LongBench) no mid-depth layer beats the own-layer default.

papers.title: Nonlinear adiabatic theorem for the Gross-Pitaevskii equation
papers.abstract: We prove a nonlinear adiabatic theorem for the repulsive Gross-Pitaevskii (GP) equation with a time-dependent trapping potential $V(x,t)$. If either (i) $V(\cdot,t)$ is smooth, subquadratic in space and with uniformly bounded spatial derivatives of order $\geq 2$, or (ii) $V(\cdot,t)$ is a uniformly bounded perturbation of a fixed non-negative potential which is asymptotically $|x|^m, m\geq 2$, then the GP equation has a global solution, which remains uniformly close to the instantaneous minimizer of the time-independent GP functional, provided the initial condition is a ground state. In fact, we show that the existence of a solution of the GP equation is the real bottleneck: If existence is assumed, then adiabaticity holds under very minimal assumptions.

papers.title: Weak and Sharp Stretched-Exponential Flocking in the Kinetic Cucker-Smale Model with Noncompactly Supported Initial Data
papers.abstract: We study the long-time behavior of the kinetic Cucker-Smale model under initial data with unbounded support in both position and velocity. Such data invalidate classical diameter-based flocking arguments and make sustained spatial cohesion difficult to establish. We prove an estimate for spatial characteristics under a finite spatial second moment and a sufficiently high velocity moment, without any requirement on coupling strength. We also prove weak flocking, i.e. control of spatial variance and integrability of velocity fluctuations in time. Under stronger assumptions on the initial tails, we establish uniform propagation of spatial exponential moments of explicitly determined order, a substantially stronger conclusion than bounded spatial variance. These estimates lead to explicit stretched-exponential rates of velocity alignment and convergence of the centered spatial distribution toward a limiting profile. Another contribution is the construction of countably atomic solutions that show optimality of the decay exponent in the spatial-tail-limited class. Together, the results clarify how initial phase-space tails govern spatial confinement and quantitative flocking for kinetic distributions without compact support.

papers.title: Ferroelectric Switching in x-cut MgO-doped Thin-Film Lithium Niobate: Implications for Periodic Poling and Domain-Wall Electronics
papers.abstract: Thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) revives a mature ferroelectric as a wafer-scale platform for integrated photonics and, increasingly, for domain-wall electronics such as nonvolatile memories and memristors. Both applications rely on controlled ferroelectric switching, which is poorly understood in TFLN: periodic poling consistently requires electric fields above 30~kV/mm, far above the coercive fields of about 21~kV/mm and 4.5~kV/mm of bulk congruent and 5~mol\% MgO-doped lithium niobate, respectively. Here, we present systematic ferroelectric hysteresis measurements on x-cut, 5~mol\% MgO-doped TFLN with coplanar electrodes as used for periodic poling, combining the positive-up-negative-down (PUND) method with second-harmonic microscopy (SHM). We obtain a spontaneous polarization of $(0.72\pm0.02)$~C/m$^2$, consistent with bulk values, while the coercive field varies between 24 and 40~kV/mm with the voltage ramp rate and depends on the electrode geometry. We identify three contributions to the high coercive fields: (i) fast voltage ramps, (ii) finger electrodes, and (iii) the coplanar surface-electrode geometry. Together with bulk data, the coercive field follows a single power law of the ramp rate over five orders of magnitude, showing that the high fields are dominated by switching dynamics rather than by intrinsic thin-film properties. Moreover, the apparent internal field depends on the electrode geometry, and reverse switching leaves buried, electrically isolated domains. These results provide guidelines for scalable, fab-compatible periodic poling---one of the principal bottlenecks of TFLN device integration---and for the write and erase operation of TFLN domain-wall devices.

papers.title: TIGER: Learning from Researcher Taste to Generate Tailored Research Ideas
papers.abstract: In pairwise comparisons where each judge chooses between an idea generated by its corresponding TIGER-8B policy and one generated by GPT-4.1, the three LLM researchers select the TIGER-8B idea in 56.6%-68.4% of 76 comparisons per researcher. PhD1 and PhD2 select the TIGER-8B idea in 19 of 30 pairs (63.3%) and 17 of 30 pairs (56.7%), respectively. All six directed cross-policy comparisons likewise favor the judge's matched TIGER-8B policy over an off-target policy, supporting the use of individual preference feedback for tailored research ideation.

papers.title: High Frequency Safeguard and Weighted Objective Scoring Bandwidth Extension
papers.abstract: Speech Bandwidth Extension (BWE) reconstructs missing high frequencies from a band-limited signal. Please note that perceptually important information is often concentrated in short high-frequency (HF) events. Therefore, an effective BWE requires both accurate HF generation and explicit control over where, how often, and in what spectral form HF energy should be produced. To address the above HF supervision, we present HFSWO, a compact complex-spectral Swin-based dual-stream adversarial framework with two newly proposed specialized discriminators: 1. High-Frequency Safeguard Discriminator (HFSD) converts excessive framewise HF-energy ratios into a differentiable safeguard-constraint penalty optimized through a projected primal--dual augmented-Lagrangian update; 2. Weighted Objective Scoring Discriminator (WOSD) learns an interpretable convex objective scoring over spectral flatness, centroid, and rolloff. Our rigorous experiments on VCTK English and MLS French datasets across multiple frequency ranges, including noisy conditions, show significantly improved perceptual scores with 74.6% fewer parameters than the existing baseline AP-BWE, establishing a new baseline in the BWE task in multilingual and multispeaker setups.

papers.title: Iterative Gumbel Planning for Continuous Control
papers.abstract: Search-based planning remains a powerful policy improvement paradigm in reinforcement learning, driving milestone successes in discrete domains. However, extending this paradigm to continuous control exposes a structural mismatch: search evaluates a finite set of action candidates, whereas continuous RL typically relies on Gaussian policies. We show that winner-action distillation into a continuous Gaussian induces a \textit{projection error} and a stepwise variance-expanding gradient tendency when the selected action is sufficiently far from the current mean. Empirically, this tendency is associated with elevated terminal variance and a return gap on the evaluated tasks. To address this, we propose \textbf{Iterative Gumbel Planning (IGP)}. By adopting a per-dimension factorized categorical policy, IGP naturally aligns the policy support with the search candidates, eliminating the projection error and reducing the residual approximation to a bounded discretization error. To bypass the combinatorial explosion of high-dimensional discrete action spaces, IGP pairs Gumbel Top-$K$ candidate sampling with an MPPI-style multi-round iterative search to refine the policy at each state. Empirically, IGP achieves state-of-the-art aggregate performance and sample efficiency on DMControl and HumanoidBench. Furthermore, it produces more stable action sequences with lower temporal variance, demonstrating its practical potential for real-world robotic deployment.

papers.title: Nonreciprocal Spherical Attention and Retrieval: Sharp Coarsening Clocks and Certified Score Correction
papers.abstract: We develop nonreciprocal spherical attention as a mathematical framework for coarsening and compressed nearest-neighbor retrieval. For two shrinking acute blocks whose centers have zero skew pairing and whose total mass ratio is subexponential in inverse temperature, we prove $\lim_{β\to\infty}β^{-1}\log T_β=1-\cosφ$, without restricting particle-count growth. An explicit three-body flow has two rigorously separated metastable exponents. For finite compression, mass centering yields a sharp $O(r^2)$ attention-output error bound at fixed temperature, with an explicit spherical-normalization correction. We formulate skew query-side score calibration as a strictly convex moment problem and derive a unique normal equation, residual-based optimization certificates, and bounded low-rank projections. A norm-aware margin objective calibrates native squared-distance rankings. Experiments use semantic retrieval data, one million visual descriptors with three codebook seeds, and a ten-million-vector FAISS IVF-PQ index with recomputed exact cosine ground truth. On SIFT1M, skew margin calibration raises native-L2 hit@10 from 0.8926 to 0.8948; symmetric calibration reaches 0.8996. The ten-million-vector index reaches 0.8827 hit@10 at 0.1794 ms per query in a four-thread batch benchmark, while validation selects no skew update. Exact streamed attention over ten million keys evaluates compressed memory on 1,024 held-out queries. Independent matrix solves, automatic differentiation, finite differences, interval arithmetic, full-flow tests, and nine Rocq-checked algebra lemmas support reproducibility. Directionality alone does not establish retrieval superiority.

papers.title: User Engagement in Visualization: A Scoping Review of 243 Research Articles
papers.abstract: User engagement is well studied in other domains. Work to date has proposed conceptual models and definitions, approaches to measurement, and factors that influence engagement in digital interactions. However, of the articles in the visualization literature that refer to engagement, few of them make evidence-based, generalizable claims, and research that does is challenging to locate due to inconsistent reporting and often lacks connection to the broader engagement literature. To address these issues and promote the consideration of the broader engagement literature, we conduct a comprehensive scoping review of visualization literature and engagement. Using scoping review methodology, we identify and analyze 243 articles that make claims about engagement with visualizations. We coded the studies conducted, literature cited, definitions provided, and claims made in these articles and analyze the codes to evaluate the quality of the work in the field and to synthesize existing findings. We find that, despite frequent references to engagement and apparent interest in the topic, the overall quality of visualization engagement research is poor, often with weak evidence, inconsistent conceptualizations, and infrequent citation of existing models, methods, or claims. We report the evidence-based claims about what engages people with visualization, including the factors of animation, interaction, and immersion, additionally describing both corroboration and apparent contradictions between these claims. Finally, we propose the COMFI framework and mnemonic for reporting important information in future engagement studies.

papers.title: A General Approach for Assessing Sensitivity to Violations of Causal Assumptions
papers.abstract: Although causal sensitivity analyses are widely used to assess the robustness of conclusions, a key limitation is that existing methods are typically developed for specific designs. This paper develops a general sensitivity analysis framework that applies to a wide range of discrete causal models and estimands by deriving sharp bounds on causal estimands as a function of the maximum proportion of the population for which the assumption is relaxed. The framework is built on the generalized principal strata approach, which allows the translation of assumptions, estimands, and data into polynomial programs. In this approach, three classes of assumptions can be relaxed: a) functional restrictions, which limit the ways that one variable can respond to another, e.g. strong monotonicity; b) exclusion restrictions, which rule out direct causal effects; c) unconfoundedness, which rules out unobserved common causes of variables. The approach produces both sharp sensitivity curves and robustness values, i.e., the smallest sensitivity level at which the sign of a causal effect stops being identified. The applicability of the method is demonstrated by generalizing existing proportion-of-violations approaches, deriving new sensitivity analysis methods for instrumental variable and selection-on-observables designs, and reanalyzing empirical results.

papers.title: When to Probe and When to Act: Clarity-Aware Risk-Adaptive Control for Interactive Driving
papers.abstract: Safe navigation in interactive traffic requires autonomous vehicles to reason about unobservable human characteristics and the reciprocal nature of multi-agent interactions. Traditional architectures often decouple prediction from planning, leading to the "Frozen Robot Problem" or unsafe maneuvers under high ambiguity because they treat risk assessment and information acquisition as independent objectives. We argue that the notion of safety should not remain static but must instead dynamically co-evolve with the system's internal confidence: the robot should actively clarify ambiguity when necessary while also recognizing the diminishing returns of information, and naturally transition toward task execution. We introduce a unified belief-space Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework that couples multistep information planning with a clarity-adaptive Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) barrier mechanism. By treating clarity, a scalar informational state, as an explicit planning variable, the controller co-designs its probing strategy with its safety specification, tightening conservatism under high ambiguity and relaxing constraints as confidence improves. We further provide a performance analysis showing that the cost of information seeking and the expected planning-cost gap to a controller that knows the true human characteristic are bounded by residual ambiguity and solver error. We evaluate the framework in lane-merging and unsignalized-intersection scenarios against representative interactive-planning baselines. Across 5,000 simulations, the proposed method achieves the highest success rates (94.6% and 93.2%) and the lowest collision rates (1.2% and 1.4%) among the compared methods, providing a principled foundation for robust decision-making in human-centric environments.

papers.title: Separating the Polar of Sets of Uniqueness from the Polars of All $H^{(d)}$-Sets
papers.abstract: We construct a perfect set of uniqueness on the circle carrying a continuous probability measure which annihilates every $H^{(d)}$-set, simultaneously for all finite dimensions d. This gives a strict inclusion between the polar of the compact sets of uniqueness and the polar of the union of the classes $H^{(d)}$, answering a question raised in earlier work on these polars. The construction uses random binary increments of size comparable to the reciprocal of a product of square roots. A Gaussian sampling estimate gives a uniform Fourier-tail bound for all pseudomeasures supported by the resulting set, and also bounded atomic approximation and spectral synthesis. A separate energy estimate, stable under deletion of a small number of increments, yields full support for every limiting quasi-independent image of every positive measure absolutely continuous with respect to the constructed measure.

papers.title: Projective relativistic dynamics from a quantum Lorentz algebra: time-dependent deformed Hamiltonians on (anti-)de Sitter spaces
papers.abstract: A (non-standard) quantum deformation of the Lorentz algebra $\mathfrak{so}(1,3)$ is used to construct novel time-dependent Hamiltonian systems on the (anti-)de Sitter spacetimes in $(1+1)$-dimensions. The specific deformation considered here contains, among others, the non-standard quantum deformation of $\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{R})$ and that of the `book' algebra $\mathfrak{b}_{2}$ as quantum subalgebras. The guiding idea is to apply the theory of Poisson--Hopf deformations of Lie--Hamilton systems to the Lorentz deformation, giving rise to a broad family of time-dependent deformed systems that share the same deformed Poisson--Hopf Lorentz algebra symmetry. In particular, this approach provides Hamiltonian vector fields expressed in terms of certain projective canonical variables, which, in turn, are related to the usual Beltrami variables via a canonical transformation. Under this construction, it is shown that the underlying Lorentizan spaces possess constant curvature $κ$ and the quantum deformation parameter $z$ can be identified with $κ$, such that the cosmological constant is $Λ=-z\equiv -κ$. Therefore, we deal with the anti-de Sitter, de Sitter and Minkowskian spaces for $z>0$, $z<0$ and $z=0$ (the undeformed case), respectively. Finally, as applications, we study time-dependent deformed oscillators on the (anti-)de Sitter spaces in detail, as well as time-dependent deformed Bateman and generalised coupled Caldirola--Kanai Hamiltonians.

papers.title: On the Conditional Consistency of the Bootstrap
papers.abstract: This paper focuses on the conditional consistency of the bootstrap. The target is the conditional law of a statistic given a common shock, and the bootstrap approximates it by the law of a resampled statistic conditional on the shock and the data. We call the bootstrap consistent if these laws are close in the Kolmogorov distance for almost every realization of the shock. The conditioning $σ$-algebras are allowed to be unrelated across sample sizes, and both the comparison law and the dimension of the data may vary with the sample size. We give sufficient conditions for consistency in this sense, show that they yield asymptotically correct conditional coverage for bootstrap quantiles, and provide a finite-sample bound on the coverage error. We also relate the Kolmogorov formulation to the merging of probability measures. The results are specialized to statistics depending smoothly on an estimator or on an estimated nuisance parameter.

papers.title: Can AI Reviewers See Your Efforts to Improve Your Paper? A Large-Scale Study of Paper Revision Trajectories
papers.abstract: AI reviewers are increasingly used to assess scientific manuscripts, yet it remains unclear whether their judgments reflect the improvements authors make through revision. We investigate this question using PaperTrajectory-2026, the 2026 release of PaperTrajectory, a dataset of 6,959 paper trajectories across five AI conferences, with automatic annotations of changes along 14 dimensions and separate judgments of overall quality. The annotations show that major improvements emphasize empirical evidence and framing, while later revisions tend toward incremental improvement. Using independent assessments of manuscript versions from eight AI reviewers, we examine whether annotated major improvements receive higher scores, which revision dimensions are associated with score changes, and whether user opinions can outweigh observed revision gains. Every reviewer leaves scores unchanged on most major improvements, and agreement on the direction of score changes is weak. Revision dimensions show some reviewer-specific associations with score increases, but provide limited predictive discrimination and no consistent guide across reviewers. Even when a revision earns a higher neutral score, a brief negative user opinion can erase or reverse that advantage, with substantial variation across reviewers. These findings show that substantive revisions are not consistently reflected in review scores and that observed scoring gains can be vulnerable to user framing, motivating assessments that connect manuscript evidence to overall judgments and remain stable when no scientific evidence changes.

papers.title: Modeling Visual Cortex with Layerwise Multiscale Manifold Capacity Maximization
papers.abstract: Task-optimized deep neural networks have risen to prominence as the most predictive phenomenological models of responses in primate visual cortex, but leave much to be desired from the perspective of biological plausibility. One such limitation is the reliance on precise credit assignment through global backpropagation of error signals. Recent work has shown that this weakness can be circumvented by requiring each subsequent stage to solve a distinct and increasingly complex task, allowing for layerwise local learning signals. We propose a novel strategy for crafting such intermediate losses that uses an efficient coding framework formulated in terms of manifold capacity, and which can be computed using a sequence of {canonical cortical computations}. In particular, we leverage the relationship between the multiscale nature of visual signals and the dilation of receptive field sizes in cascaded visual representations to modulate complexity, allowing for the reapplication of these common loss computations at each stage of the hierarchy. We evaluate our approach on its ability to predict neural datasets spanning three areas of the ventral stream hierarchy in macaques, as well as human psychophysical data on an object classification task. We find that our unsupervised layerwise model matches or exceeds the performance of competitive architecture-matched baselines on all evaluations considered.

papers.title: Direct and Indirect Competition in a Two-Prey-One-Predator System : Global Dynamics, Chaos, and the Paine Conjecture
papers.abstract: This paper studies the global dynamics of a three-dimensional Lotka-Volterra system of two prey, with direct competition between them, and one predator. Under a symmetry assumption, the rescaled parameter space is sorted into four generic categories, which yield a complete classification of the global dynamics into 56 meaningful subcases. We determine the existence and stability of the boundary and positive equilibria, including global asymptotic stability and bistability of boundary equilibria, and necessary and sufficient conditions for local asymptotic stability of the positive equilibrium. We identify regimes of periodic solutions and chaos, including a period-doubling route to chaos. We further show that the parameters of Gilpin's chaotic dynamics fall within some cases. Biologically, we introduce the notion of extensive negative competition, which, together with trade-off competition and apparent competition, interprets the interactions among the three species. Our classification shows that the full system largely tracks the dynamics of the prey-only subsystem, and these competition mechanisms explain the differences between them, clarifying how predator-mediated interactions alter competitive outcomes and facilitate prey persistence, thereby providing mathematical support for Paine conjecture.

papers.title: Omitting Types for Infinitary Real-Valued Logic: A Topological Perspective
papers.abstract: For countable vocabularies, we extend the omitting types theorem for countable fragments of infinitary logic to Keisler's general real-valued structures by proving that the space of Henkin types of each such fragment is Čech-complete. The structures interpret function symbols arbitrarily and predicate symbols by bounded real-valued functions, while each formula carries a bound of its own. This extends the setting of Eagle's theorem from metric structures with a prescribed master metric to general structures whose vocabulary prescribes the sorts and bounds of the symbols. Following Keisler and Miller's treatment of logic without equality, we build models from closed terms. Morley's Baire category method then gives every satisfiable theory on a countable fragment a model with countable sorts omitting any countable family of types whose closed-term instances have empty interior in the space of Henkin types satisfying the theory.

papers.title: Metamorphic Testing for Evaluating Robustness of Sentiment Analysis Models
papers.abstract: Machine learning systems are challenging to test using traditional software testing methods because their behavior is learned from data rather than explicitly programmed. This challenge is particularly significant in natural language processing (NLP), where small input variations can lead to unexpected model behavior. Conventional evaluation metrics, such as accuracy and F1-score, often fail to capture such inconsistencies. Metamorphic testing addresses this limitation by evaluating expected relationships between original and transformed inputs. With the increasing prevalence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and language-based AI systems, the need for systematic robustness testing has become even more pronounced. Motivated by this growing need, this paper presents a lightweight, batch-based metamorphic testing approach for evaluating the robustness of such systems. In particular, we consider sentiment analysis as a representative NLP task and evaluate a pretrained classifier under four transformations: synonym replacement, typo injection, word-order variation, and negation. Using consistency score, flip accuracy, and confidence change, we identify strengths in handling semantic variations and vulnerabilities to textual noise and logical transformations. These findings highlight the value of metamorphic testing in identifying behavioral inconsistencies beyond conventional performance metrics and demonstrate its potential as a systematic framework for evaluating the robustness of language-based AI systems and guiding performance improvements before deployment.

papers.title: How the eigenvalue region of standardized Laplacians leaves the 2005 polygon
papers.abstract: Let $Λ_n$ be the set of all eigenvalues of $n\times n$ standardized Laplacian matrices, and let $S_n\subseteqΛ_n$ be the polygon introduced in 2005, with upper vertices $λ_0=0,\dots,λ_{n-1}=1$. It is now known that $Λ_n=S_n$, and that $Λ_n$ is convex, if and only if $n\le4$. We study how $Λ_n$ leaves $S_n$ near an edge $[λ_m,λ_{m+1}]$, $2(m+1)<n$. First, we prove a switching law for matrices having a boundary point of $Λ_n$ as a simple eigenvalue: an explicit switching function on the arcs, built from the left and right eigenvectors and the outward normal, forces maximal weight where positive and zero weight where negative; intermediate weights occur only where it vanishes. Second, we perturb the weights of the arcs $k\to k+m+1$ in the circulant digraph (arcs $k\to k+s$, $1\le s\le m$, plus these arcs with weight $τ$) that realizes the point $λ_m+τ(λ_{m+1}-λ_m)$. At second order, the first Fourier harmonic of the perturbation moves the eigenvalue beyond the line of the edge if and only if $τ<τ^*_m=\sin(πm/n)/(2\cos(π/n)\sin(π(m+1)/n))$. For even $n$ and $m$, the point with $τ=τ^*_m$ is the vertex of $S_{n/2}$ lying on this edge, and digraphs with these arcs only at even $k$ give an explicit eigenvalue path that leaves $S_n$ at $λ_m$ and, in all computed cases, ends at this vertex. Third, we give a conjectural, numerically supported picture of $\partialΛ_5$: beyond each edge of $S_5$ not incident to $0$ or $1$, $Λ_5$ forms a cap bounded by four algebraic arcs, which leaves the edge tangentially at its endpoint adjacent to $0$ or $1$ and rejoins it at $τ^*_1=(3-\sqrt5)/2$; the rest of the edge lies on $\partialΛ_5$. In computations for $n\le8$, a cap returns to its edge smoothly at $τ^*_m$, at a corner at $τ^*_m$, or at a corner beyond $τ^*_m$.

papers.title: Q-BWE: Quantum Chaos-Informed Speech Bandwidth Extension
papers.abstract: High-frequency reconstruction in bandwidth extension (BWE) depends on joined interactions among nonlinear spectral, temporal, and perceptual features; assigning a separate discriminator to each such feature may be redundant and may fail to model their joint interactions. We introduce quantum-informed generative model Q-BWE, where we design a five-qubit Quantum Chaos Discriminator (QCD) instead of using separate discriminator for every features, for modeling nonlinear joined-feature interactions efficiently. Our QCD explores a compact five-qubit quantum-inspired inductive bias based on data re-uploading circuit, trainable controlled NOT (CNOT) rotations, quantum entangling gates, and statevector measurement map. Five features for five qubits are selected from a 26-dimensional speech-dynamics bank and are encoded by a two-layer statevector circuit, producing 31 measurements map of local behavior, correlations, mixedness, and Born entropy. QCD guides a Lattice-ConformerNeXt generator with FiLM conditioning and a cosine-masked residual pathway, while delayed-reward Thompson sampling adaptively controls its contribution. The circuit is simulated on classical hardware. Overall, Q-BWE achieves competitive performance on VCTK English, and MLS French datasets in multilingual and multi speaker setups under clean and noisy conditions across a broad set of evaluation metrics with approximately 1.72x fewer parameters (33.5M vs. 19.4M) compared to recent CIS-BWE baseline published in ACL.

papers.title: Retrain, Alert, or Rollback? A Three-Response Decision Framework for Production ML Under Concept Drift
papers.abstract: When a deployed model degrades under concept drift, an operator can retrain it, raise an alert and monitor, or roll back. Yet most drift-adaptation methods consider only retraining. We present RAR (Retrain-Alert-Rollback), a state machine that gives each response an explicit trigger and cost. Retraining is gated on drift detection, label availability, and measured degradation. Every retrained model must pass a two-stage canary before promotion, and corruption-triggered and quality-triggered rollbacks enter different hold states. Under a prospectively specified protocol we compare RAR with six baselines, including a cost-aware retraining policy, on 13 streams: eight real public streams and five semi-synthetic streams derived from them. RAR does not dominate. At low retraining cost, retrain-heavy baselines lead, and no policy's rank differs significantly from RAR's. At higher cost, RAR beats detector-triggered retraining, periodic retraining, and no response simultaneously on four streams, each within a bounded cost window. Its advantage over detector-triggered retraining is consistent with a latency-feasibility condition stated in advance. Against the cost-aware policy, results are heterogeneous. RAR retrains before true drift onsets one eighth to one third as often as detector-triggered retraining, but at lower net utility on most semi-synthetic streams. On H2's designated corruption stream (a registered follow-up), rollbacks fire yet RAR loses to retraining baselines. At $ρ= 1$, removing the canary, and thus rollback, raises utility on 11 of 13 streams. On a post-hoc follow-up stream, cause-specific hold release resumes adaptation where a single cooldown does not. We provide the harness, configurations, and per-cell results for reproduction.

papers.title: $P$-stationary structural equation modeling: Causal effect identification under temporally incomplete observations
papers.abstract: Causal modeling of discrete-time processes often involves the assumption that the modeled processes are stationary. A general class of linear causal models for discrete-time stationary processes are structural equation processes (SEP), which generalize the well known structural equation model for i.i.d. observations. In this paper, we extend the SEP model from stationary to $P$-stationary processes, which are non-stationary processes whose $P$-periodically sampled subprocesses are jointly stationary. We will use this model to approach the problem of causal effect identification under temporally incomplete observations from a graphical modeling perspective. To have a notion of generic identifiability, we restrict our analysis to $P$-stationary structural vector autoregressive (SVAR) processes, which are SVAR processes whose underlying coefficients can vary $P$-periodically over time. Our findings allow to detect, in any given temporally incomplete observational setting, if a certain set of instrumental processes qualifies to identify a causal effect between $P$-periodic subprocesses, and if this is the case, that effect admits an explicit expression as a rational function evaluated at the observational spectral density.

papers.title: Calibration-Constrained Diagnostics for Evaluating LLM Self-Evaluation
papers.abstract: We introduce a reusable evaluation artifact for diagnosing whether LLM self-reported confidence can support confidence-gated act-or-defer decisions. The artifact is designed for evaluation rather than safety certification: it provides a black-box protocol, prompts, judge-reference labels, model outputs, reproduction scripts, and calibration-constrained diagnostic metrics for auditing LLM self-evaluation across math, factual, and commonsense reasoning tasks. Our central finding is that aggregate uncertainty summaries can produce deployment-misleading rankings: a model that appears strongest under standard aggregate calibration metrics can fail under category-level calibration constraints, while a model with worse aggregate calibration can exhibit stronger calibration-constrained behavior in the positive-margin region where high self-selection accuracy and tight calibration coexist. To expose this failure mode, we define PVC and C-PVC as category-level diagnostics over an accuracy-by-calibration surface: PVC counts categories whose self-evaluation accuracy exceeds a threshold, while C-PVC additionally requires category-level calibration error below a tolerance. We aggregate these diagnostics using Volume Under Surface (VUS) and a positive-margin restriction; they are VC/fat-shattering motivated but are empirical evaluation proxies, not literal VC-dimension estimates. Across 13 models and four benchmarks, the artifact shows weak confidence-correctness separation, stable diagnostic rankings under alternative categorizations and judge-label perturbations, and persistent positive-margin failures not captured by ECE or Brier score. Confidence-gated self-evaluation therefore requires calibration-constrained, category-level diagnostics, and we provide a reusable artifact for applying them under black-box access.

papers.title: Partial Invariance for Classification under Structural Causal Models
papers.abstract: Making predictions in an unseen environment from data collected across multiple training environments is challenging. This challenge is particularly pronounced when the target-generating mechanism varies across environments. In this work, we introduce environment-label separation, a form of partial environmental invariance that decomposes the target conditional distribution into an environment-invariant component and a label-invariant component. We show that this partial invariance enables estimation of the target conditional distribution in an unseen environment when using labeled training data together with unlabeled test features. Within the structural causal model framework, we provide sufficient conditions for environment-label separation. Building on these conditions, we develop an algorithm, dIMP-Classifier, which jointly minimizes an estimate of the test risk and encourages invariance across environments. We further provide finite-sample guarantees that characterize the test risk in terms of deviations from invariance, estimation error, and sample complexity. Experiments on simulated data and the real-world light tunnel Causal Chamber data demonstrate that the proposed approach can perform under interventions on the target mechanism and consistently outperforms the considered standard and invariance-based baselines.

papers.title: Multiclass Classification with Rare Useful Features: Fundamental Limits and the Optimality of Diversity Pursuit Higher Criticism Thresholding
papers.abstract: We consider classification in high-dimensional feature spaces where only a vanishing fraction of features are useful and the number of classes may be large. While this rare-and-weak useful-feature regime is well understood in the binary setting, its multiclass version raises new questions: a feature can be useful for class discrimination without separating any specific pair of classes. We focus on a rare feature diversity model, in which most features are useless, but a small fraction promote discrimination among classes in a way that can be detected by a per-feature diversity test, such as one-way ANOVA or the Kruskal-Wallis test. For this setting, we propose Diversity Pursuit Higher Criticism Thresholding (DP-HCT), a feature-screening procedure that applies a higher-criticism threshold to the collection of p-values obtained from per-feature diversity tests. We justify DP-HCT under a Gaussian multiclass Rare-and-Weak Useful Feature model with class-mean contrasts of fixed magnitude in random directions, extending the binary model of Donoho and Jin (2008). When the number of classes is fixed, our model recovers the binary phase transition. When the number of classes grows logarithmically with the number of features, however, we derive a new and strictly harder phase transition, driven by the growing degrees of freedom and their effect on the useful-feature tail rate.
